…including 4.5kW motor, bigger 1.4kWh battery and 45mph top speed
Yozma may not have invented the mini moto space, but they certainly helped mainstream it. Together with Tuttios and Sur Rons,
Yozma’s IN10
was one of the most popular mini motos out there, and if you surveyed the average group of 14-15-year-olds in a suburban rideout, you’d be hard-pressed not to find at least a few Yozma IN10s among them…
Today Yozma is shipping the IN 11
, which attempts to bridge the gap between entry-level mini-bikes and high-end off-roaders, but at what cost?
Taken in a vacuum, the Yozma IN11 is an impressive update to the IN 10 and actually is more closely specced to the bigger
IN10 Pro
Yozma IN 11 spec sheet:
Peak motor output, up sharply from the prior IN 10’s 2,600W baseline.
Claimed peak torque, delivering aggressive low-end climb performance.
Advertised top speed in Race mode. Real world only slightly lower
52V 27Ah = 1404Wh:
Removable lithium battery pack, promising up to 55 miles of range in Eco mode with a 5- to 6-hour recharge time. No one has time to drive for 55 miles in Eco Mode. Expect 20-30 miles when gunning it.
~$1,299:
Pre-order and promotional launch pricing. Yozma has the swag to demand a higher price point than the sub-$1,000 off-brand offerings, but it isn’t a slam-dunk decision.
Auto Wheelie Assist:
Embedded in “Stunt Mode,” this feature allows riders to cap front-wheel elevation between 15° and 40° with anti-tip protection, functioning like digital training wheels for lofting the bike. Wheelies also increase the likelihood of injuries obviously
One-button reverse gear
– helps riders maneuver tight trails and tight garage spaces without manhandling the frame.
Brake Light /
Magnetic kill switch
– nice safety features and substitute for key in some cases.
Tiered riding modes:
Four maps (Eco, Sport, Race, Stunt) let users toggle between commuter battery conservation and full-torque delivery.
But we of course, don’t live in a vacuum, and others, including the
Heybike Villain
Engwe Eagle
have already brought 52V, 4.5kW motors to the pit bike form factor, sometimes at much lower cost.
I should say here that parents who want to keep their kids’ e-motos in the 20-30mph range are going to be a whole lot happier with the 2.6kW than 4.5kW motors. Two nice safety improvements over the original Yozma IN10 include the magnetic kill switch and brake lights on the IN11.
Electrek’s take: Yozma’s advantages
If we are keeping it real here, there are dozens of similar-sized and spec’d mini-e-motos out there, often at a
much lower cost
than the Yozma IN11. But I’d argue that as the biggest and most trusted of these brands, Yozma is a safer bet.
Also, the IN11 is just a lot more solid than the random Amazon/Alibaba electric pit bike. Putting the IN11 together is quicker and easier than any other emoto I’ve built, and it just feels a lot more solid.
That feeling extends to the safety features. The brakes are more dialed in. The turning feels a lot tighter, and the overall ride is quieter and lighter. I believe, and my limited testing bears this out, that spec for spec, I got a lot more range on the IN11 than I got on other bikes with similar battery and motor specs. That 200nm of torque feels like it belongs on a much more expensive e-moto.
The wheelie mode is a nice trick (15, 25, or 40 degrees wheelie settings) and something
we’ve only seen on Anylands
for this price point so far. It is more developed on the IN11 but expect to see this on just about every new pit bike coming out over the next few years.
That said, the price, which is currently fluctuating between $1299 and $1499 (don’t forget your $60 off
Electrek
code), Yozma is going to be on the more expensive side of the 4.5kW emotos out there and some of the
newcomers are bringing an intense value competition
to the place where Yozma once dominated by itself.

title: Austria allocates 173 MW at average price of €0.0642/kWh in PV tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Austria’s third solar market premium auction of 2026 attracted 195 successful bids, with a volume-weighted average price of €0.0642/kWh, slightly higher than in the previous round.
Ralph Diermann
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
A solar park in Austria
Austria’s Renewable Energy Expansion Act (EAG) funding agency has published the results of the country’s third auction for solar PV market premiums in 2026. Successful bids ranged from €0.054/kWh to €0.0725/kWh, with a volume-weighted average of €0.0642/kWh, slightly higher than in the second auction round.
The auction offered 172.6 MW of solar capacity, but ultimately awarded 173.4 MW across 195 successful bids. The EAG funding agency did not disclose the level of oversubscription.
The bidding round closed on Sept. 24, 2026. Unsuccessful applicants can submit new bids in future auctions, although no further dates have been announced.
Austria’s solar market premium auctions are open to new ground-mounted and rooftop PV installations, as well as extensions of existing systems, with capacities exceeding 10 kW. Projects must not have been commissioned at the time of bidding. Ground-mounted installations on agricultural land or grassland are subject to a reduction of up to 25% in their applicable bid value, a measure designed to favor rooftop PV projects.
Austria’s second solar market premium auction, which closed on June 11, 2026, offered 179 MW of capacity. The EAG funding agency awarded contracts on July 10, with successful bids reaching a maximum of €0.0669/kWh. The ceiling was lower than the highest successful bid of €0.0725/kWh recorded in the third round, indicating an increase in the upper end of accepted bid prices.
The first auction of 2026 closed on March 17, with authorities awarding 170.97 MW against an offered volume of 175 MW. Successful bids ranged from €0.0400/kWh to €0.0680/kWh, with a volume-weighted average of €0.0634/kWh, slightly below the €0.0642/kWh recorded in the third auction.
The government had initially allocated 175 MW to each of the year’s four planned solar market premium auctions, although the capacity available in individual rounds can change. Under Austria’s auction framework, projects compete on their requested support levels, with bids ranked from lowest to highest until the available capacity is allocated.

title: Italy awards full 30 MW quota in second floating PV tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Italy’s second FER2 auction for floating solar projects on inland waters has allocated its entire 30 MW quota, following weak participation in the first round. Eight projects secured capacity, while two were excluded despite offering a 2% discount on the reference tariff.
Massimiliano Tripodo
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Enel’s floating PV testing facility in Catania, Italy
Italy’s second competitive bidding round for floating photovoltaic systems on inland waters under the FER2 incentive scheme has allocated its entire 30 MW quota. According to rankings published by Italian energy agency Gestore dei Servizi Energetici (GSE), two projects were excluded despite offering a 2% discount on the reference tariff.
The result marks a turnaround from the
first FER2 floating solar tender
, which allocated capacity to just one 991 kW project out of a 50 MW quota. The Italian authorities subsequently
reduced the quota to 30 MW for the second round
Of the eight successful projects, seven have capacities exceeding 1 MW and offered discounts ranging from 2.010% to 3.25% on the reference tariff.
The largest project is a 5.5 MW floating PV installation proposed by Sunprime Agira in Landiona, in the province of Novara, Piedmont. The project secured capacity with a 2.010% discount on the reference tariff of €70.6 ($82.0)/MWh.
The smallest successful project is a 380 kW installation proposed by Gens Srl in Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. It secured capacity with a 2% discount on the reference tariff of €84.7/MWh.
Rosa Rinnovabili secured allocations for five projects in Lombardy, located in the municipalities of Pioltello and Mediglia, in the province of Milan.
For the second round, reference tariffs for floating PV systems on inland waters were set at €87.3/MWh for installations between 1 kW and 300 kW, €84.7/MWh for systems between 300 kW and 1 MW, and €70.6/MWh for installations exceeding 1 MW.
In the previous round, reference tariffs stood at €90/MWh for installations between 1 kW and 1 MW and €75/MWh for systems exceeding 1 MW.
In an official notice, GSE said developers of successful projects must submit their incentive applications through the FER-E portal within 30 calendar days of the plants entering operation. The agency will notify unsuccessful applicants of the reasons for their exclusion.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Italian company unveils seven-layer PEM electrolyzer assembly to reduce iridium use - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Another 100 companies wrote the European executive body to preserve EU green hydrogen targets. Meanwhile, the European Commission selected 77 net-zero projects, including several hydrogen projects.
Sergio Matalucci
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Hydrogen
UFI Hydrogen’s new generation of proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs)-
UFI Hydrogen
has unveiled a new generation of proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) at Hydrogen Technology World Expo in Hamburg, Germany. The Italian company, part of the UFI Group, said the platform integrates seven functional components into a single assembly, compared with three in its existing MEA technology, to reduce iridium consumption and simplify stack manufacturing. While conventional three-component MEAs require electrolyzer manufacturers to source, integrate and qualify additional components separately, the new architecture is designed to reduce supplier interfaces and streamline procurement, testing and qualification. The company said the reduction in iridium use is achieved through improvements in MEA architecture, functional components and catalyst configuration, although it has not disclosed specific catalyst loadings or performance figures. The platform can also be customized to manufacturers’ stack requirements, including geometries, dimensions, membrane characteristics, catalyst selection and component interfaces. “The MEA is the chip of electrochemistry: it is where a decisive share of an electrolyzer’s performance and competitiveness is determined,” said CEO Marco Lazzaroni. The company aims to work directly with electrolyzer manufacturers on the design and qualification of customized assemblies, reducing integration risks. The new product is undergoing industrial scale-up, with testing, validation and integration activities planned with stack manufacturers. Series production is scheduled to begin in 2027, while UFI Hydrogen’s existing three-component MEA technology will remain in production.

Signatories include European companies Axpo, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), Iberdrola, De Nora, Ingeteam, Siemens Energy and Snam, as well as non-European companies Adani, Acwa Power, Air Products, Hitachi, Masdar and Toyota.

The commission also selected a Belgian project to scale up solid oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) technology and an Italian project to expand solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) and SOEC manufacturing. Several large-scale projects, primarily involving refineries, will focus on increasing low-carbon hydrogen production and consumption.

The facility has been producing hydrogen since 2023. “The upgraded 6.5 MW system sits within the same plant. From the outside, the only visible addition is an extra converter cabinet. At nominal load, the facility can now produce up to 1,270 Nm³ of hydrogen per hour,” said the two Danish companies.

The company said it had made progress toward a possible restart during a suspension of payments, including reaching agreements with customers, continuing projects and holding advanced discussions with prospective investors. “Although it was not possible to finalise all necessary agreements within the available timeframe, the progress achieved provides a valuable foundation for the next phase,” Resato said.

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: Polysilicon inventories remain high - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
TrendForce said China’s polysilicon inventories remained above 560,000 metric tons despite expected production cuts in October. Persistent oversupply and weak downstream demand continued to weigh on prices.
Vincent Shaw
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
TrendForce
’s EnergyTrend said on Oct. 22 that polysilicon inventories in China remained above 560,000 metric tons, despite an expected month-on-month decline of approximately 20,000 metric tons in domestic production in October. Supply continued to slightly exceed demand from downstream ingot manufacturers. EnergyTrend said polysilicon producers had discussed maintaining selling prices at or above CNY 43 ($6.32)/kg, although the proposed price floor does not necessarily reflect actual transaction prices. Elevated inventories and weak downstream demand continued to weigh on prospects for a sustained price recovery.
, a Chinese renewable energy data provider, said centralized solar module procurement tenders totaled approximately 6.6 GW between Oct. 3 and Oct. 16, up from 410 MW in the preceding two-week period. The increase was largely driven by major procurement programs from state-owned enterprises. Meanwhile, projects with announced contract awards or shortlisted bidders totaled 2.81 GW, down 35.4% from 4.35 GW in the previous period. The figures, released on Oct. 19, point to a recovery in tendering activity following China’s National Day holiday, while contract awards remained relatively subdued.
China’s Vice
Minister of Ecology and Environment Li Gao
said on Oct. 21 that China plans to raise concerns about unilateralism and trade protectionism at the COP31 climate summit in November. Li called for the free flow of green and low-carbon products and technologies, warning that trade barriers could undermine global climate action. Chinese solar modules and other clean energy products have faced increasing trade restrictions in the United States and Europe in recent years, putting the relationship between climate policy and trade measures in focus ahead of the summit.
National Energy Administration
(NEA) issued implementation guidelines on Oct. 21 to promote the integration of coal-fired power generation with renewable energy. The guidelines outline five integration models, including coordinated power transmission from renewable energy projects and coal-fired power plants, cleaner heating through combined heat and power facilities, and the integration of renewables with captive coal-fired generation. The measures encourage coal plant flexibility upgrades, transmission capacity expansion, and coordinated operations with wind and solar projects to improve renewable energy integration. Eligible projects may qualify for financial support under existing government programs. The policy aims to facilitate additional renewable energy deployment while reducing emissions from coal-fired generation.

title: South Korea’s renewable energy capacity overtakes coal for first time - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Renewable energy capacity in South Korea reached 41 GW on Oct. 21, edging past coal-fired capacity for the first time, according to the country’s power market operator.
Brian Publicover
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Seoul, South Korea
South Korea’s installed renewable-energy capacity has surpassed coal-fired capacity for the first time, reaching 41,040 MW on Oct. 21, according to the Korea Power Exchange. That is 283 MW more than the country’s 40,757 MW of coal-fired capacity.
Renewables now account for 25.4% of South Korea’s installed generation capacity, making them the country’s second-largest source of installed capacity after liquefied natural gas (LNG), at 46,788 MW. The gap between renewables and LNG has narrowed to about 5,748 MW, said KPX.
Renewable capacity grew by an average of about 3,504 MW a year between the end of 2020 and the end of 2025, about 4.3 times the roughly 807 MW added annually for LNG. KPX said that if both trends continue, renewables could overtake LNG within two to three years to become South Korea’s largest source of installed generation capacity. The Export-Import Bank of Korea said it expects
South Korea to install 3.5 GW of solar
in 2026.
The figures refer to installed capacity rather than electricity generation.
KPX said it will support the government’s target of
100 GW of renewables by 2030
Grid expansion
The milestone follows a
government plan to expand grid capacity for renewables
. It aims to raise national transmission-level hosting capacity for renewables from 119 GW to 171 GW by 2030 and distribution-level capacity from 84 GW to 110 GW.
The plan also allows solar projects to connect above normal grid limits, with output curtailed when the network is constrained, and raises the solar connection limit on a distribution line from 14 MW to 16 MW and at a substation from 50 MW to 60 MW. Under the plan, grid connection rights will be linked to a reformed renewable portfolio standard (RPS) from January 2027, with access granted to projects selected through competitive bidding rather than on a first-come, first-served basis.

South Korea’s solar additions
surpassed 3.1 GW in 2024

title: Sodium-ion storage maker Peak Energy raises $108 million in GM-led round - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A US sodium-ion battery storage company has closed a $108 million Series B round led by General Motors’ venture arm, as it prepares to start production at a 4 GWh factory in California and launch its systems in the data center market.
Brian Publicover
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Peak Energy said its oversubscribed Series B was led by GM Ventures, with participation from Maverick Silicon, Infinite Capital, Eclipse, Xora Innovation and LG Technology Ventures. The company did not disclose its valuation or the size of GM Ventures’ contribution.
Peak Energy said the funding will help it scale domestic manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders and launch its passively cooled sodium-ion systems in the data center market. The round follows a
$55 million Series A in 2024
“The investment we announce today will supercharge Peak’s ability to scale and deliver as the world increasingly turns to passively cooled sodium-ion storage to solve our energy needs,” said Landon Mossburg, Peak’s co-founder and chief executive officer.
Order book
Peak Energy has not broken down the $1 billion figure. Its largest disclosed deal is a
multi-year phased agreement with Jupiter Power
for up to 4.75 GWh between 2027 and 2030, starting with about 720 MWh in 2027 and including an option for a further 4 GWh from 2028 to 2030.
In February, Energy Vault signed what it described as a
definitive supply agreement for 1.5 GWh
of Peak Energy systems, alongside a joint development agreement for storage serving AI data centers. Neither company has named an end customer or site. Peak Energy has also agreed to
pilot a sodium-ion system with RWE’s US business
in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) market, though no capacity was disclosed.
When Peak
announced its factory in July
, it said it had more than 6 GWh of customer commitments.
Cell supply
Peak Energy said its 183,000-square-foot Sacramento plant is designed for up to 4 GWh of annual output, with production scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The company has put the capital investment at about $71 million.
The company currently sources cells from manufacturers in China, built to its specifications, and assembles them into containers at its facility in Burlingame, California. In June, it
partnered with GM
to co-develop next-generation sodium-ion cells with the carmaker’s Michigan battery labs.
“GM Ventures is investing to help Peak Energy continue to scale this innovative technology because we believe it has significant potential in the energy storage market as a safe, cost-effective solution using abundant, domestically sourced materials,” said Kevin McCabe, president of GM Ventures.
Peak Energy said its system, which eliminates active cooling, can cut the cost of energy by up to 20% compared with conventional storage and requires zero planned maintenance. The claims have not been independently verified.
The company
unveiled its first grid-scale system
in July 2025 at the Solar Technology Acceleration Center (SolarTAC) test facility in Colorado, and
began operating
the 3.5 MWh installation that September with nine utilities and independent power producers. It had earlier set up a
sodium-ion cell engineering center
in Colorado.

title: Transaera tests its heat pump with metal-organic framework dehumidification in apartment building - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
U.S. startup Transaera will test its all-electric rooftop heat pump system in a multifamily residential building in Washington, D.C., with support from a $125,000 grant. The technology uses metal–organic frameworks for dehumidification and reportedly cuts energy consumption by around 40% compared with conventional rooftop HVAC units.
Emiliano Bellini
23 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
Residential
Transaera installation on a multifamily building in Washington D.C.
U.S. startup
Transaera
announced it will test rooftop heat pump technology in a multifamily residential building in Washington D.C., United States.
The project is backed by a $125,000 grant from the National Deployment Grant Fund of The Clean Fight, a New York-based nonprofit that supports the early deployment of proven clean energy technologies.
“Building owners deciding how to electrify need operating cost reduction and want to see performance data from a building like theirs before they commit,” said Sorin Grama, CEO and co-founder of Transaera. “This project lets us prove, with independent data, that a more efficient system works as well to properly condition a whole apartment building as it does in an Amazon warehouse. Working with the largest apartment owner in the country means those results will go directly to the people making these decisions.”
The company describes its technology as a dedicated outdoor air system (DOAS), a type of heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) system that conditions incoming outdoor air for ventilation separately from a building’s primary heating and cooling equipment.
The all-electric system combines cooling, heating and dehumidification in a single platform. Operating as a heat pump, it eliminates the need for gas-fired reheating while managing both sensible and latent cooling loads in commercial buildings.
According to Transaera, a key feature of the technology is its approach to humidity control. Unlike conventional HVAC systems, which typically cool air below its dew point to remove moisture through condensation before reheating it, the DOAS uses solid desiccant materials based on metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) to extract moisture from incoming air before cooling. By separating dehumidification from the cooling process, the system is designed to reduce energy consumption and improve overall efficiency.
The company claims the technology can reduce energy use by approximately 40% compared with conventional packaged direct expansion (DX) rooftop units. It is also designed to maintain efficient operation in hot and humid climates, where high latent cooling loads make humidity management particularly challenging.
Transaera has designed the system as a drop-in replacement for conventional rooftop HVAC units. According to the manufacturer, its dimensions and weight are comparable to those of existing equipment, allowing installation within standard rooftop footprints without major structural modifications. The system can also be maintained using standard HVAC servicing procedures, eliminating the need for specialized technician training.
The technology is primarily aimed at large commercial buildings, including warehouses and logistics facilities, where managing humidity and high latent cooling loads can be particularly demanding.

Our work with Transaera has moved from field trial to readiness for first commercial use, and this new collaboration supports expanding use of this technology within our global network of buildings,” said at the time Asad Jafry, Director of Global Energy, Sustainability and AGV at Amazon.

title: European solar, BESS marketplace expands to Romania - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solmeria, an online marketplace for selling solar and battery energy storage systems directly to buyers, is now listing projects in Romania alongside offers in France and Italy.
Patrick Jowett
23 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
European renewable energy marketplace Solmeria has expanded to include solar and battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Romania.
The marketplace, which spans ground-mounted PV, agriPV, C&I solar and BESS projects at all stages of development,
initially went live in July
with 25 projects in France.
It added its first two listings in Romania earlier this month. The two offers are both agrivoltaic installations with four-hour storage systems located in Cluj county, northwestern Romania. They have a combined capacity of 6.2 MW of solar and a total BESS capacity of 6 MW/24 MWh.
Maxime Courtaigne, CEO of Solmeria, told
pv magazine
the Romania listings now also include a ready-to-build hybrid park of 55 MWp with 193 MWh of storage. “The first listings have already received around ten expressions of interest from buyers,” he added.
Created at the request of developers, the marketplace is aiming to bring liquidity to listed projects, accelerate transactions and reduce intermediation costs. Commission is only payable only upon successful completion of a sale and is significantly lower than that of a traditional merger and acquisitions agency, according to previous reports.
Courtaigne also told
pv magazine
18 of the 25 French projects listed in the marketplace are now in sale discussions. The marketplace also opened in the Italian market in September.
He added there are more than 300 registered acquirers to date, the majority of which are French and Italian, with “dozens more joining every month.”
“France showed us that selling projects one by one to the right buyer works at every size: a 1 MWp project drew 35 expressions of interest,” Courtaigne said.
“Romania is on the same path, with around ten already on our first listings and a 55 MWp hybrid park now on the platform. Sell one project to the right buyer, and the portfolio will follow.”

title: Hemispherical perovskite solar cell design reduces sensitivity to sunlight angle - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers have designed a hemispherical perovskite solar cell with a textured surface to improve light absorption and reduce sensitivity to sunlight incidence angles. Simulations showed absorption exceeding 95% and an average maximum power output of 28.25 mW/cm² across incidence angles of 0° to 50°.
Lior Kahana
23 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Illustration of a hemispherical perovskite solar cell with a textured outer surface
A research team in China has proposed a hemispherical perovskite solar cell with a textured surface designed to reduce sensitivity to the angle of incident sunlight. The hemispherical geometry is intended to enable radial charge collection, while the textured surface scatters incoming light in multiple directions to enhance absorption and promote more uniform charge generation.
“Perovskite solar cells have attracted intensive research interest as a promising candidate for next-generation photovoltaic technologies, offering high power conversion efficiency and low manufacturing cost,” the researchers said. “However, the practical energy yield of conventional planar perovskite cells is severely compromised by optical losses under varying solar incidence angles, leading to significant power fluctuations that undermine their viability for renewable energy generation.”
To evaluate the design, the researchers modeled five cell architectures: planar, nanowire, smooth hemispherical, and hemispherical structures with rounded-cone or textured rounded-cone front surfaces. Each device consisted of an indium tin oxide (ITO) electrode, a phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) electron transport layer, a methylammonium lead iodide (CH₃NH₃PbI₃) perovskite absorber, a nickel oxide (NiO) hole transport layer, and a silver (Ag) rear electrode.
The researchers used Lumerical software to simulate the five architectures, analyzing light absorption, scattering, electromagnetic fields, and charge generation across wavelengths ranging from 300 nm to 800 nm and incidence angles from 0° to 50°. They then incorporated the resulting charge-generation profiles into electrical simulations that accounted for carrier transport and recombination. The simulations were used to calculate current-voltage characteristics, power conversion efficiency, and maximum power output under different illumination angles.
Across incidence angles ranging from 0° to 50°, the textured rounded-cone cell achieved an average short-circuit current density of 25.47 mA/cm², compared with 24.03 mA/cm² for the smooth hemispherical cell and 22.52 mA/cm² for the planar device. It also achieved an average maximum power output of 28.25 mW/cm² and light absorption exceeding 95%.
“The design effectively decouples device performance from incident light angle, overcoming the critical challenge of angular-dependent power output,” the researchers concluded. “The three-dimensional hemisphere symmetry enables balanced carrier transport, while the Mie resonances induced within the perovskite shell ensure efficient light trapping.”
The solar cell concept was presented in the study “
Angle-robust photovoltaics via Mie resonance hybridization for stable power output in perovskite solar cells
,” published in
Solar Energy
. The research team included scientists from China’s Jilin Normal University and the
Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Panasonic begins sales of glass-based perovskite solar panels - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Panasonic began commercial sales of its glass-based perovskite solar panels in September 2026, ahead of the planned launch of full-scale mass production in April 2029. The initial products are manufactured at the company’s development facility in Moriguchi, Osaka Prefecture.
Vincent Shaw
23 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The mass-produced products, scheduled for launch in April 2029, will feature larger dimensions of up to 1.8 m × 1.2 m and additional glass thickness configurations of 4 mm x 4 mm and 5mm x 5 mm.
Japanese electronics manufacturer
Panasonic Holdings
announced it will start full-scale mass production of
glass-based perovskite solar panels
for applications in building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) one year ahead of schedule.
The company had originally planned to start production in fiscal year 2030, which in Japan runs from April 1, 2030, to March 31, 2031.
“Ahead of full-scale mass production, we began commercial activities in September 2026 by selling pre-production products manufactured at Panasonic HD’s development facility in Moriguchi, Osaka Prefecture,” the company said in a statement. “Going forward, we aim to establish mass-production technologies at our Nagahama facility and accelerate market development through the commercial deployment of these initial products.”
“Panasonic HD was selected for a Green Innovation Fund project by the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) in September 2025 and has since been developing mass-production and installation technologies for glass-based perovskite solar cells,” it went on to say. “Given the progress in these technologies, growing market demand, and supportive government policies, the company has decided to bring forward the start of full-scale mass production from its original schedule.”
The modules’ graphic patterns
Panasonic said its pre-production glass-based perovskite solar panels feature a laminated-glass structure, with maximum dimensions of 1.8 m × 1.0 m and glass thickness configurations of 3+3 mm or 6+6 mm. The products are available with float glass or high-strength glass and support customized decorative designs.
The mass-produced products, scheduled for launch in April 2029, will feature larger dimensions of up to 1.8 m × 1.2 m and additional glass thickness configurations of 4+4 mm and 5+5 mm. They will also be available in laminated insulating glass configurations, with tempered glass offered as an additional option.
According to the company, both product generations comply with Japanese building standards and have passed internal tests based on IEC 61730 and IEC 62790. Panasonic also said it plans to pursue module certification in line with customer requirements and market developments.
The company uses inkjet coating, laser processing and glass encapsulation technologies in the manufacturing process. It said the technology enables customized dimensions, transparency levels and decorative patterns, making the products suitable for building-integrated photovoltaic applications, including windows and facades.
Panasonic did not disclose the modules’ power conversion efficiency, rated power output, temperature coefficient, expected service life or pricing.
The Japanese electronics manufacturer has been developing perovskite solar technology for more than a decade. In 2020, the company
unveiled a lightweight perovskite solar module
with a power conversion efficiency of 16.09% and an area of 802 cm², manufactured using an inkjet coating process.
In 2023, it
began testing glass-based perovskite solar panels
in a building in Fujisawa, Kanagawa Prefecture, in cooperation with property developer Mitsui Fudosan Residential. The company subsequently achieved a certified efficiency of 18.1% for an 802 cm² device.
More recently, in December 2025, Panasonic and Japanese building materials manufacturer YKK AP
tested the technology in office windows
, focusing on installation methods and design flexibility.
The commercialization efforts come as the Japanese government seeks to establish a domestic perovskite solar industry. In November 2024, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
announced a target
of deploying around 20 GW of perovskite solar capacity by 2040.
The government also outlined plans to support domestic manufacturing and reduce production costs to JPY 14 ($0.09)/W by 2030 and JPY 10/W by 2040. In September 2025, the Ministry of the Environment
introduced subsidy programs
to support early deployment of perovskite solar cells and their integration with battery storage systems.
Japan has since stepped up its support for the technology. In May 2026, NEDO
opened a supplementary funding call
under its Green Innovation Fund to advance mass-production technologies for single-junction perovskite solar cells.
In September, the Ministry of the Environment
announced plans
to exclude conventional silicon solar panels from newly introduced subsidy programs starting in fiscal 2027, prioritizing perovskite and other next-generation solar technologies. The policy shift is intended to strengthen Japan’s industrial competitiveness and accelerate the commercialization of emerging photovoltaic technologies.

title: Schrödinger’s toy hidden-variable model revealed in unpublished manuscript
content: An unpublished, undated manuscript belonging to Erwin Schrödinger lies in the Austrian Central Library for Physics at the University of Vienna. Physicist Flavio Del Santo at the University of Geneva retrieved it and analyzed its contents to establish a likely date it was written and also what the famous physicist thought about random outcomes in quantum physics. The draft is titled ‘Collapse of Determinism’ and addresses one of the major problems in quantum physics – randomness of events. Quantum theory is usually used to predict the probabilities of measurement but never specific outcomes. Physicists have wondered whether this is a result of incomplete knowledge of the domain. For instance, the outcome of a coin toss seems random at first. However, if one has information about how hard the coin was tossed and the speed of the wind in the area of the toss, then there is reliable information to predict the outcome too. In the quantum realm, much remains uncertain. However, if particles carry information that determines their behavior, would they become more predictable or deterministic? What famous physicists thoughtThe debate between determinism and indeterminism in quantum mechanics has split the physicists into two groups that stand strongly by their views. While Einstein, David Bohm, and Schrödinger are often seen as champions of determinism in scientific history, Santo argues that there stance was more nuanced and less polarised than many think. Schrödinger’s unpublished manuscript is a case in point. Quantum particles carrying information that could determine their behavior is termed hidden variables, since this information might not be accessible for scientists to observe it. In 1932, mathematician John von Neumann published a result that suggested that hidden variables should not be added to quantum mechanics, During World War II, Taylor Whittaker, a British physicist and mathematician, questioned determinism, invoking Neurman’s work and citing an example of polarized light passing through a polarizer. In this setup, the angle between the polarized light and the polarizer determines how much light can pass through the latter. Quantum mechanics expresses the outcome as a probability. However, Whittaker used two values for hidden variables in this hypothesis and argued that these could not reproduce the changes that were created when the polarizer was turned. Schrondinger’s manuscript is a response to this assumption. What Schrödinger wroteIn his three-page manuscript, Schrondinger questions the restriction built into Whittaker’s reasoning and wonders why hidden variables had only two possible values. Instead, he suggested an alternative where each photon was assigned a value between zero and one. The numbers were distributed evenly across the incoming beam, and whether the photon passed the polarizer depended on its number and the polarizer’s angle. Across photons, the setup reproduced the expected transmission rate, which can be predicted using Malus’ law, but each individual outcome depended on the apparatus setting and the proposed number of the photon. Schrodinger’s manuscript also solves the problem that arises after the first measurement, where the distribution changes. So, he created a mathematical rule that changes the photon’s number after it is transmitted or reflected and restores the distribution as per Malus’ law. The question then remains is why did Schrödinger not publish this? According to Del Santo, this was likely because Heinrich Pelzer, an Austrian physicist, challenged Whittaker in a published paper. Although Pelzer’s approach was different, it still made the same point. Del Santo warns that the manuscript must not be used to claim that Schrondinger sided with a deterministic view of nature. This unpublished work could be a test of an argument rather than endorse the model, Del Santo wrote in a analysis paper. This paper can be found on the preprint server arXiv.

title: US nuclear fusion push tackles high-voltage limits in semiconductors
content: Nuclear fusion promises virtually limitless clean energy, but building a mini-star on Earth requires extreme electronics. In this regard, American fusion developer Helion has taken a major step toward solving that bottleneck.The Washington-based company has reached a preliminary agreement with the US Department of Commerce for up to $175 million in federal funding. Backed by the CHIPS Act, the grant is matched by $50 million from private investors.Together, the $225 million package will fund domestic facilities and production lines to help build the specialized modules needed to run commercial fusion reactors.Utilizing high-power pulsed electrical systemsHelion’s approach relies on high-power pulsed electrical systems. These circuits must repeatedly capture, switch, and release colossal surges of electricity in fractions of a second. At present, the robust semiconductors required for these tasks are only made abroad.By manufacturing them in the United States, Helion hopes to eliminate overseas supply chain risks. The new designs are intended to run at higher voltages, stay cooler under stress, and operate reliably for years.“Building fusion power plants at scale requires us to accelerate technologies like semiconductors that are critical to making fusion possible,” said David Kirtley, chief executive of Helion. He noted that the new funding will help produce chips that meet the precise efficiency and performance standards the company needs.Protecting public moneyThe investment will be split across two primary hubs. Everett, Washington, will receive over $100 million to build research facilities and power module manufacturing lines. The project will focus on advanced packaging techniques that bundle multiple chips into compact units.A further $80 million will head to Burlington, Vermont. Working with an industry partner, Helion will design specialized tooling and production machinery to support high-volume manufacturing. The rest of the funds will go toward automated assembly systems.In an unusual arrangement designed to protect public money, the federal government will take an equity stake in Helion. Under the preliminary agreement, the Department of Commerce will receive $175 million worth of non-voting shares, pegged to the company’s recent Series G valuation.US officials say the domestic chip facilities could also yield wider benefits. Bill Frauenhofer, an executive director at the Department of Commerce, pointed out that breakthroughs in high-power switching will aid national power grids and defense applications.Push toward commercial nuclear fusionThe funding lands during an intense push toward commercialization. Helion recently closed a $500 million investment round and reported plasma temperatures of 150 million degrees Celsius. Earlier this year, Washington state regulators issued key radiation and air permits, giving Helion clearance to construct the generator building for its flagship plant, named Orion.Fusion generates power by fusing light atomic nuclei such as deuterium and helium, releasing huge energy without long-lived radioactive waste. While Helion has yet to publish peer-reviewed results confirming net electricity generation, it faces an ambitious commercial deadline: delivering 50 megawatts of power to Microsoft data centers by 2028.“Delivering American-made fusion energy to the grid could fundamentally change US strategy from managing energy scarcity to harnessing clean energy abundance, unlocking new industries, strengthening national security, and improving quality of life for all Americans,” concluded Helion in a press release.

title: US Abrams tank launches Switchblade kamikaze drones with upgraded kit
content: General Dynamics Land Systems has unveiled PERCH 2.0, an upgraded launcher kit that equips M1A2 Abrams tanks and Stryker armored vehicles with AeroVironment Switchblade 300 loitering munitions. The system is designed to give vehicle crews extended-range surveillance and the ability to strike targets beyond their direct line of sight.PERCH, short for Precision Effects & Reconnaissance, Canister-Housed, was developed in partnership with AeroVironment. The latest version, announced by General Dynamics on social media, introduces changes intended to improve the system’s integration with armored vehicles and expand its reconnaissance and strike capabilities.The company says PERCH 2.0 supports beyond-line-of-sight surveillance and over-the-horizon lethality using Switchblade 300 variants, letting crews identify threats and engage targets farther away without exposing their vehicles to direct fire.Bringing loitering munitions to armored vehiclesThe Switchblade 300 is a small, tube-launched loitering munition that can be used for reconnaissance and precision strikes. After launch, it can remain airborne while its operator searches for a target, then directs the aircraft toward it.By integrating the weapon into a vehicle-mounted launcher, PERCH is intended to give tank and armored vehicle crews an organic reconnaissance and strike capability. Instead of relying entirely on dismounted troops or external reconnaissance assets, crews could use the drones to observe areas beyond the vehicle’s immediate field of view.General Dynamics said PERCH 2.0 supports extended-range surveillance and anti-armor strikes using the Switchblade 300 Block 20 (18-mile range), as well as strikes against softer targets using Block 10 and Block 20 variants.The system also supports target handoffs between vehicles and between mounted and dismounted forces, according to the company. This could help units share information as they move through complex terrain, although the announcement does not detail the precise communications architecture or the conditions under which these handoffs take place.Updated design frees up space on the AbramsOne of the changes highlighted in the PERCH 2.0 announcement is its more space-efficient configuration. General Dynamics says the upgraded system returns 41% of the sponson-box volume compared with the original PERCH design.PERCH 2.0 💥 Our Precision Effects & Reconnaissance, Canister-Housed technology, created in partnership with AV, has been upgraded for 2026. The PERCH common modular kit integrates onto M1A2 Abrams SEPv3 tanks and Stryker vehicles to provide beyond line of sight (BLOS)… pic.twitter.com/nD6zlijGUJ— General Dynamics Land Systems (@GD_LandSystems) October 21, 2026On the Abrams, the sponson box is a storage compartment mounted along the side of the turret. Replacing or adapting this space for a drone-launching system introduces a trade-off between adding new capabilities and retaining room for equipment and supplies.The original PERCH kit was designed to attach to existing vehicle mounting points without requiring welding or cutting, according to previous descriptions of the system. Its modular approach is intended to simplify integration while avoiding major modifications to the host vehicle.The upgraded kit is intended for the M1A2 Abrams SEPv3 and Stryker vehicles, extending the concept beyond heavy tanks to wheeled armored platforms.From field trials to an expanded capabilityThe original PERCH system was demonstrated during a US Army obstacle-breaching exercise at Fort Hood, Texas, in October 2025. During the Machine Assisted Rugged Sapper event, an Abrams equipped with the system launched Switchblade 300 and Switchblade 600 munitions to support reconnaissance and targeting ahead of troops negotiating an obstacle.That demonstration showed how vehicle-launched drones could support forces operating in difficult terrain. PERCH 2.0 now emphasizes the Switchblade 300 family and improvements to the launcher’s packaging and capabilities. By combining protected mobility with remotely operated surveillance and precision-strike options, PERCH could help crews detect and respond to threats without moving the vehicle directly into view of the target.

title: NEURA's 20% lighter humanoid robot heads toward mass production
content: NEURA Robotics has unveiled 4NE1 Gen 4, a humanoid robot designed for serial production that is 20 percent lighter than its predecessor.The robot features a slimmer design, a black textile outer skin, advanced motion control, and Neuron AI, the company’s foundation model for Physical AI. The launch coincides with the opening of the TUM RoboGym, a joint research and training center NEURA and the Technical University of Munich (TUM) established near Munich Airport. The 2,300-square-meter facility will train robots for practical tasks using real-world data, human demonstrations, and simulation.4NE1 gains intelligence4NE1 Gen 4 is a humanoid robot designed for serial production that is 20 percent lighter than its predecessor. The robot features a slimmer body, a black textile outer skin, advanced motion control, and Neuron AI, the company’s foundation model for Physical AI.The 4NE1 Gen 4 represents the latest generation of NEURA’s humanoid robot platform. Its redesigned body is slimmer and lighter, while its black textile outer skin provides a different exterior finish from the previous generation.The robot incorporates advanced hands for more precise gripping and Smart Limbs, which allow individual limbs to respond independently to their surroundings. According to NEURA, these features are intended to help the robot react quickly and move more fluidly.At the core of the system is Neuron AI, NEURA’s Perception-Language-Action model for Physical AI. The model translates the robot’s perceptions into movements, using inputs that include vision, touch, force, sound, and the robot’s internal state.These capabilities are intended to help robots handle tasks that require more than visual recognition. For example, a robot may need to determine whether a fastener has clicked into place while assembling a component.Neuron AI is trained using real-world robot data, human demonstrations, and simulation. Through NEURA’s Neuraverse platform, skills learned by one connected robot can be shared with others in the network.The company is preparing 4NE1 Gen 4 for serial production. The robot is already operating at NEURA Gyms, where companies can train and test practical applications.4NE1 Gen 4 is already making its mark on the world stage. 🤖 Today, we unveiled the next generation of our humanoid robot on two major stages. First, at the opening of the TUM RoboGym powered by NEURA in Munich, built in collaboration with the Technical University of Munich… pic.twitter.com/ljBlmHQTU7— NEURA Robotics (@NEURARobotics) October 22, 2026Training smarter robotsThe TUM RoboGym provides a shared environment where researchers and companies can develop robotic capabilities for manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, healthcare, and other industries.Companies provide specific tasks and process knowledge, while researchers investigate how robots can learn them faster and perform them more reliably. Training activities began in September, with participants from more than ten industries, including automotive, pharmaceuticals, medical technology, packaging, logistics, agriculture, and care.Demonstrations involve tasks such as handling cardboard boxes, filling bottles, and loading and unloading wooden components. Companies can use the facility to evaluate robot systems, identify training requirements, and assess applications before expanding their deployment.The training infrastructure combines three approaches. Real-world robot data captures movements, physical contact, and task outcomes through sensors. Human demonstrations use sensor-equipped suits, motion-capture systems, and teleoperation to record movements and interactions. Simulation expands this experience by exposing robots to additional situations and variations before testing their skills on physical machines. According to NEURA, the center supports multiple robot types, including humanoids, mobile assistance robots, and cognitive robot arms.NEURA and TUM have committed to an initial three-year partnership, with a combined investment of approximately €17 million. NEURA is contributing about €11 million, along with robotics infrastructure, computing resources, and operational support.Munich is also the starting point for NEURA’s planned international network of training centers, with additional locations planned in Europe, the United States, and China. NEURA is also developing another German facility with RWTH Aachen.

title: Ultra-thin coatings could pull CO2 from air in less than one second
content: Researchers at Switzerland’s Empa research institute are developing a direct air capture technology that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in cycles lasting less than one second. The approach replaces bulky porous filters with ultra-thin, amine-containing coatings that can rapidly absorb and release CO₂.The technology is part of Empa’s Mining the Atmosphere research initiative, which explores ways to capture atmospheric carbon and turn it into reusable materials and chemicals. Researchers have conducted initial flow and process simulations, but experimental testing is still needed to determine whether the approach can compete with existing direct air capture systems.Thin coatings could speed up carbon captureDirect air capture systems typically move large volumes of air through porous materials that bind CO₂. The captured gas is then released, often by heating the material and applying a vacuum or steam. Because atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are only around 430 parts per million, these systems must process large volumes of air to collect meaningful amounts of the greenhouse gas.Empa’s approach takes a different route. Rather than maximizing the amount of CO₂ captured in each cycle, the researchers aim to capture smaller quantities much more frequently.The proposed system uses ultra-thin coatings made from amine-containing materials. Instead of allowing CO₂ to penetrate deep into a porous adsorbent, the coating binds it at or near the surface. This reduces the amount of material that must be heated during the release stage.“The process can be significantly accelerated thanks to the low thermal mass,” Empa researcher Dirk Hegemann explained in the institute’s announcement.The thin layers can heat up and cool down quickly, allowing adsorption and desorption, the capture and release of CO₂, to alternate at much shorter intervals than in conventional systems. Empa researcher Sandra Galmarini says the target is to complete a cycle in less than a second, compared with several minutes for conventional approaches.A moving surface could continuously capture CO₂The proposed design resembles a conveyor belt. A continuously moving surface coated with the capture material passes through two zones.In the first, ambient air flows across the coating, allowing CO₂ to bind to its surface. In the second, the material is heated under reduced pressure, releasing the captured gas and preparing the coating for another cycle.Separating these stages allows each zone to operate under different conditions. The capture section needs sufficient airflow, while the release section benefits from a small gas volume to reduce the energy required for heating and creating a vacuum.The researchers also see potential advantages in the system’s modular design. Multiple smaller units could be combined rather than building increasingly large and complex capture facilities. The moving surface might also help transport air, potentially reducing the energy required by fans.Experimental testing remains a key hurdleDespite the promising simulations, the researchers have not yet experimentally demonstrated the proposed sub-second capture cycle. Empa says a new measurement platform is needed to determine how quickly CO₂ binds to and separates from the thin coatings.The team also needs to evaluate how much CO₂ the system can capture per unit of volume and time, whether the coatings remain stable through repeated cycles, and how well seals and pressure zones perform at high rotational speeds.Hegemann is functionalizing surfaces with plasma coating, while the broader research team is developing the experimental setup needed to test the process.The central challenge is whether the speed advantage can translate into meaningful overall performance. Capturing less CO₂ per cycle means the system must operate rapidly and repeatedly to achieve competitive throughput without consuming excessive energy for heating, cooling, airflow, and vacuum generation.If those challenges can be addressed, the technology could offer a more flexible approach to direct air capture.

title: Retired US Navy helicopters find new life as sensor testbeds for Army
content: The U.S. Army has begun flight testing four MQ-8C Fire Scout unmanned helicopters, repurposing aircraft retired by the U.S. Navy to test Army sensors while avoiding more than $70 million in procurement costs. The helicopters, originally destined for long-term storage, will help engineers evaluate sensor packages under realistic flight conditions.The Army’s Redstone Test Center at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, received the helicopters along with two mobile control systems, spare engines, and support equipment. After completing ground tests in August 2026, the team began flight testing at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah and Redstone Arsenal.Retired Navy helicopters find a new roleThe Navy started retiring its MQ-8C fleet in February 2024, and the last aircraft will leave service by the end of fiscal 2026. The Multi-Mission Tactical UAS program office, called PMA-266, had already started sending aircraft and equipment to the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group in Tucson, Arizona, often known as the military’s aircraft boneyard.In November 2024, the Redstone Test Center approached the Navy about using the helicopters as captive-carry testbeds. This method allows engineers to mount sensors on an aircraft and collect flight data without releasing the payload. It also provides a way to evaluate equipment without procuring a dedicated test aircraft.Army and Navy personnel inspected the helicopters and control systems at Point Mugu, California, in December 2024. The Army formally requested four aircraft, two control systems, spare engines, and support equipment in January 2025.Transfer recovers equipment and cuts costsThe Navy approved the request in May 2025, and the aircraft and control systems reached Redstone Arsenal by July that year. The program office also worked with Naval Supply Systems Command to recover communications security equipment, including radios, transponders, and modems. The final recovered assets arrived in July 2026.The transfer saved the Army more than $70 million in procurement costs. The Navy also said the arrangement avoided additional spending on research and development, flight hours, data collection, contracts, equipment sourcing, and manpower.“Considering where we started—having zero experience with these systems—it’s quite remarkable what has been accomplished. We are certainly thankful for the many people across various organizations that helped us along the way,” said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Taylor Kiel, a test director and experimental test pilot with the Redstone Test Center’s Aviation Flight Test Directorate.Flight tests prepare crews and maintainersThe ongoing tests will help Army personnel become familiar with the aircraft before they begin sensor evaluation work. The program also gives maintainers practical experience with the helicopters and their associated systems.The Navy said the transition took 14 months from the Army’s initial request to the start of flight testing.“Our priority is delivering lethal and ready capabilities to the warfighters,” said Col. Leigh Irwin, PMA-266 program manager. “Repurposing these MQ-8C assets from storage to active testing is a major acquisition win for both services, demonstrating how we can supercharge existing capabilities and increase acquisition velocity to support joint operations.”MQ-8C brings long-endurance flight capabilityNorthrop Grumman built the MQ-8C Fire Scout using the airframe of the commercial Bell 407 helicopter. It was designed to operate from Navy littoral combat ships and other vessels that can handle aircraft.The unmanned helicopter provides surveillance and targeting support, with an endurance of up to 12 hours and a range of approximately 173 miles (150 nautical miles). The Navy achieved initial operational capability with the MQ-8C in June 2019 and purchased 38 aircraft. By 2023, it operated only 10, while the remaining helicopters sat in storage.The four transferred aircraft are now undergoing flight testing as the Army prepares to use them for sensor development and evaluation.

title: X-59 supersonic jet flies at Mach 1.4 speed in milestone NASA test
content: For nearly 11 years, test pilot Mike Lippert pushed high-performance aircraft to maximum performance. But one ultimate career milestone kept eluding him. He had never flown an X-plane. And he ultimately got an opportunity to fly one on October 21.Soaring high above California’s Mojave Desert, Lippert finally realized his lifelong ambition by taking control of NASA’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft for the first time.The flight is a key triumph for both the pilot and NASA’s mission to reshape the future of commercial air travel.A dream decades in the makingLippert launched from NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. And stayed airborne for exactly one hour.During the flight, the sleek research jet reached a top speed of Mach 1.4 while cruising at 55,000 feet.“After completing our high-altitude test points, there was a brief period where we descended and decelerated, where I was able to look outside and recognize that I was flying supersonic in an X-plane over the high deserts of the Mojave,” Lippert recalled. “It was a special moment for sure.”While the X-59 has taken to the skies before, getting Lippert ready for his maiden flight required months of preparation.He didn’t do it alone. Working closely alongside fellow NASA test pilots Nils Larson and Jim “Clue” Less, Lippert spent countless hours in ground simulators mapping out every potential variable. In August, he performed his first engine run inside the cockpit, honing communication routines with the mission control team.That meticulous ground prep paid off. Lippert smoothly executed complex maneuvers to test the jet’s handling and system integrity.For Lippert, the achievement was as emotional as it was technical.“This flight was very special to me,” Lippert said. “For as long as I can remember, I’ve dreamt of doing exactly what I got to do today, testing a truly unique aircraft and working with the exceptional people on this test team.”NASA’s Quesst missionThe aircraft made a triumphant return to the skies following a routine maintenance check and a comprehensive system review. This ground inspection followed its most intensive operational stretch yet, during which the crew completed six flights in just three days. Building on that momentum, engineers approved the jet for its next major milestone.The X-59 has a unique, needle-like nose designed to disperse shockwaves, and cuts the need for a forward windshield. Pilots like Lippert navigate using an External Vision System (XVS) that streams a virtual 4K forward view to an internal cockpit monitor. Interestingly, the aircraft was built from repurposed parts from established fighter jets, such as a T-38 canopy and ejection seat, along with F-16 landing gear. These measures helped to reduce development time and costs. A single General Electric F414 engine powers the experimental jet, producing 22,000 pounds of thrust with afterburners to drive its supersonic research flights.The primary objective of NASA’s Quesst mission involves conducting test flights with the X-59 over various US communities to measure public reaction to quiet supersonic sound. Researchers plan to share these acoustic findings with aviation regulators to establish data-driven noise standards. This evidence could eventually persuade authorities to repeal the decades-long ban on commercial overland supersonic travel.

title: Silicon-rich battery cells retain 83% capacity after 1,000 full cycles
content: Silicon can store far more charge than graphite, but keeping silicon-rich batteries working over repeated charging cycles remains a hurdle to industrial use. Researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE have now tested pouch cells that retained over 83 percent of their original capacity after more than 1,000 full cycles.Announced on October 20, the StrOboBatt project results came from in-house-manufactured, 25-Ah cells with silicon-rich anodes. The research cells achieved an energy density of 280 Wh/kg, advancing high-energy batteries for electric mobility, aerospace, and stationary storage.The results also highlighted an operating requirement: mechanical pressure significantly affected the cells’ ability to maintain performance.Tackling silicon’s durability hurdle“Cycle life is one of the key hurdles to the widespread industrial use of silicon-rich anodes. More than 1,000 cycles with a capacity retention of at least 80 percent is considered an important performance target here,” said Dr. Lukas Dold, team leader for battery materials technology and scaling at Fraunhofer ISE.The team manufactured multilayer full cells containing 40 layers, using commercially available electrode foils. These paired a silicon-carbon/graphite anode with a nickel-rich nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide cathode.Silicon has a theoretical specific capacity ten times that of graphite, the material currently used in battery anodes. In the test cells, a silicon-carbon composite accounted for 51 percent of the anode active material.The anodes achieved a specific capacity above 1,000 mAh/g and an areal capacity exceeding 5 mAh/cm².Fraunhofer ISE expects an industrially optimized pouch cell format to reach approximately 330 Wh/kg. That figure is a projection; the demonstrated energy density was 280 Wh/kg in the institute’s non-optimized PrecISE research format.A high-energy pouch cell with a silicon-dominant anode, manufactured at Fraunhofer ISE, in its aged state after 1,000 full cycles. Credit: Fraunhofer ISEPressure shapes battery performanceResearchers tested the cells at axial contact pressures of 300 and 1,000 kilopascals during 1C charging and discharging. Regular check-up cycles at lower current rates helped them evaluate how pressure influenced cycle stability.External pressure can improve interfacial resistance and reduce the risk of electrode materials separating from one another or their substrate, an issue particularly relevant to silicon-containing anodes.“Axial pressure has a significant impact on the long-term behavior of the cells. At a contact pressure of 1,000 kPa, our cells still retain over 83 percent of their original capacity even after more than 1,000 full cycles,” explained Marc Kissling, group leader for battery cell production and technology evaluation at Fraunhofer ISE.Cells operating at 300 kilopascals showed a greater decline in usable capacity, particularly during 1C operation.Moving toward industrial validationThe team also observed a growing gap between residual capacity measured at low discharge rates and capacity available during regular 1C operation. Capacity retention alone therefore does not fully describe these cells’ operating performance.Manufactured on a semi-automatic cleanroom production line, the pouch cells serve as references for evaluating materials, designs, and operating conditions.Fraunhofer ISE’s infrastructure covers electrode mixing, roll-to-roll coating, cell assembly, formation, and electrochemical characterization. This lets researchers assess new battery concepts throughout the manufacturing process while examining the conditions needed to sustain performance.

title: 311 miles in five minutes: China unveils 1.44 MW EV charging system
content: Five minutes plugged into a charger could add 311 miles of driving range, according to Chery, which has announced a 1.44-megawatt system as competition intensifies across China’s electric vehicle industry. The automaker’s Volt-Dragon technology can also charge a battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in six minutes and 50 seconds.The announcement comes as Chery showcases its integrated energy technologies at the 2026 International User Summit, held October 19–23 in Wuhu, Anhui. More than 2,000 international guests and users are attending the event to explore how the company connects electricity generation, storage, and consumption.Adding range in minutesThe claimed output puts Chery among the Chinese manufacturers developing megawatt-class charging technologies. However, peak power alone doesn’t show how quickly every compatible vehicle will charge.Chery’s result places it 23 seconds behind CATL’s reported six-minute, 27-second benchmark for reaching 97 percent charge.Under what Chery described as conservative scenarios, delivering the same range would take eight minutes. The company did not disclose specific results for very cold or very hot conditions during the announcement.Its CheryMind system adjusts power in response to temperature changes within the battery. Chery presents this AI-powered control as a way to support charging speed while protecting battery health.These performance figures remain company claims. The supplied announcement does not specify the vehicle, battery capacity, or range-testing standard used.Connecting vehicles to the gridChery’s smart energy center combines solar generation, battery storage, and charging infrastructure into a local microgrid. The company describes it as China’s first large-scale AC vehicle-to-grid demonstration station.The installation also powers a renewable-energy rest area where visitors can stop to charge their vehicles. Its island mode maintains charging during grid disruptions, according to Chery.Bidirectional vehicle-to-grid technology allows compatible EVs to draw electricity during lower-priced, off-peak periods and return it during peak demand. This two-way flow can help manage energy costs, balance grid loads, and improve the use of renewable electricity.Where supported, vehicles can also supply homes and communities during outages, extending their role beyond transportation.For residential users, Chery offers its Energy Cube system, which integrates rooftop solar, batteries, and bidirectional charging to increase the use of self-generated electricity.Expanding beyond passenger vehiclesChery has implemented a similar microgrid at an electric heavy-duty truck park in Spain, pairing renewable generation with storage and high-power charging for freight operations. The company expects this overseas deployment to provide a model that can be replicated to meet local industrial needs. However, the supplied material does not quantify the installation’s operating savings or emissions benefits.Its broader energy portfolio includes long-cycle-life Rhino batteries and research into solid-state technology. Laboratory samples have shown high stress tolerance, supporting further safety testing for automotive and residential applications.Meanwhile, Chery’s public charging network is still taking shape. The company says an initial 100 chargers across 10 Chinese cities will open soon, followed by a planned expansion to 20,000 stations worldwide by 2029.

title: US' 1-MW nuclear microreactor to be deployed at naval weapon station
content: A California-based company’s microreactor has been selected by the U.S. Navy for deployment at Naval Weapons Station Crane, Indiana. Radiant’s Kaleidos microreactor — a factory-built, transportable 1-megawatt microreactor transportable by land, sea, or air — has been selected for the deployment.“There is not an organization in the world with more experience in nuclear power than the U.S. Navy,” said Tori Shivanandan, President and Chief Operating Officer of Radiant. “We are honored to be selected by the U.S. Navy for this important work and we thank the Navy and the Army’s Dr. Waksman for their confidence in Radiant to deliver reliable, resilient nuclear power wherever their mission demands. Our mission of Atoms for Prosperity is today strengthened by the support of the Navy and the State of Indiana.”Transportable nuclear power to militaryThe Navy’s selection marks another major milestone in Radiant’s drive to bring transportable nuclear power to military and commercial customers. Radiant is the only nuclear company partnered with the Army, Navy and Air Force, underscoring military confidence in Kaleidos and Radiant’s ability to deliver mission-ready nuclear power.“The Department of War is actively breaking down the barriers that have prevented deployment of nuclear reactors,” said Mike Dodd, Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies. “The selection of Radiant for NWS Crane represents a critical acceleration in our mission. We are not just investing in technology; we are leveraging vital commercial capabilities to deliver an immediate, asymmetric advantage directly to the warfighter.”Kaleidos reactor provides up to five years of powerThe company revealed that plug-in ready, Kaleidos reactor provides up to five years of power before refueling across a twenty year life. Unlike permanently installed nuclear facilities that require long lead times and site-specific construction, Kaleidos provides energy in a box. It requires no cooling water, no major excavation, and no extensive on-site construction. Kaleidos gives customers a dependable source of prime power that works independent of the grid, reducing exposure to external power disruptions assuring mission continuity.Radiant’s Kaleidos reactor is undergoing the country’s most rigorous test campaign at the Idaho National Laboratory DOME facility. Following a competitive selection process, the Department of Energy awarded Radiant exclusive access to the facility for a full year. Kaleidos is undergoing the industry’s only full-scale, full-power, extended duration reactor test- using the same reactor design and custom spec’d fresh fuel that will be used for customers deployments. By testing the reactor under real-world operating conditions, Radiant is demonstrating the performance, reliability and readiness required to deliver resilient, deployable nuclear power to America’s warfighters, according to a press release.“Our installations are foundational warfighting platforms and ensuring their resilience is essential to supporting the Fleet,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By investing in advanced capabilities like this microreactor at Crane, we are providing our Shore infrastructure with the resources needed to sustain the mission and empower our warfighters.”The project will advance through design refinement, prototype testing, environmental review, site preparation and regulatory coordination before deployment. Radiant will work with the Navy, Army, DIU, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and other partners, with technical expertise and support from the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program. Safety, physical security and environmental requirements will guide the project throughout its lifecycle, as per the release.

title: 3D-printed objects could sense human movement with MIT's new software
content: Researchers have developed software that enables 3D-printed objects to sense and respond to human movements. The system, called X-Hinges, automatically embeds sensors and conductive pathways made from different materials to improve signal accuracy and reduce interference.The software allows users to customize objects by connecting shapes and selecting up to three axes of movement, with sensors placed at bending points to track motion. The approach could enable interactive devices, including robotic hands, household objects, toys, and object-detection systems.Improves motion sensingX-Hinges, developed by researchers at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Tianjin University in China, is a design software that enables 3D-printed objects to sense motion and respond to human interaction. The technology integrates sensors and conductive pathways directly into objects during fabrication, allowing them to detect movement across multiple axes.The system addresses a key challenge in manufacturing interactive objects: interference between sensor-generated electrical signals and conductive pathways. By using different materials for these components, X-Hinges improves sensing accuracy and lets objects capture multiple types of movement at once.The researchers demonstrated the technology through several prototypes, including a glove that transfers human hand movements to a robotic hand, an adaptive lamp that responds to touch, and a device that identifies objects using tactile data.Sensors detect physical changes, such as bending or compression, and convert them into electrical signals. Conductive pathways carry these signals through the device to electronics that process the data.When both components use the same conductive material, their electrical responses can become difficult to distinguish. This interference can reduce sensing accuracy and make it harder for a device to determine how a particular section has moved.X-Hinges addresses the problem by automatically incorporating two different materials into the design. One forms the sensors and is selected to produce strong signals, while the other creates conductive pathways designed to minimize interference. This separation helps the system distinguish sensor readings more reliably, enabling objects to respond to human input in real time.The software also provides an interface for creating interactive objects by selecting and connecting shapes and defining how their components move. Users can choose cylinders, rectangles, thin outlines, or custom geometries and specify up to three axes of movement.For example, a robotic hand may need its fingertips to move vertically and sideways. X-Hinges can embed sensors at the joints to capture movement along both axes, providing data that can help another robotic hand reproduce the user’s movements.Sensing through printingThe researchers used X-Hinges to develop a glove that records the bending of a user’s finger joints and transmits motion data to a robotic hand. Designed to accommodate different hand sizes, the glove could help robots learn grasping movements from human demonstrations, potentially supporting applications in factories and homes.Another prototype is a foldable lamp that detects when someone pinches it closed and adjusts its brightness accordingly. The team also created a tactile sensing device capable of identifying objects, such as a banana, based on sensor data collected when an item is placed on it.A video game controller shaped like a cartoon shark demonstrated the software’s ability to accommodate custom designs. The researchers configured its tail to move up and down, allowing it to function similarly to a joystick.Despite these capabilities, X-Hinges faces a calibration challenge. Small variations in the arrangement of electrical components during 3D printing can cause apparently identical objects to produce different sensor readings. To address this, the researchers developed a computer vision system that recalibrates sensor outputs to improve consistency between devices. They hope to develop an integrated recalibration mechanism in future versions.The work builds on earlier efforts to create 3D-printed mechanisms capable of movement. The team’s longer-term goal is to combine sensing and actuation within a single printing process, allowing objects to both perceive interactions and perform physical actions.
