title: New method captures rare earth material from industrial wastewater
content: US researchers have developed a sponge-like material to capture rare earth elements from industrial wastewater.​Rather than simply treating wastewater, a Rice University team viewed dirty water pools as resource pools to recover valuable rare earth materials. It could eventually open the possibility to recover critical minerals that are limited in supply in different regions.​”Instead of viewing industrial wastewater only as something that needs to be treated, we can begin thinking of it as a resource containing valuable materials that may be worth recovering,” said Qilin Li, the Karl F. Hasselmann Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Rice and corresponding author of the study.Metal-ligand chemistry​The idea may sound simple; however, it is not easy.​Besides the rare earth elements, the industrial wastewater is loaded with other metals in much higher concentrations, like iron, sodium, and aluminum. These high concentrations make it challenging to separate the minuscule amounts of the trace elements. Hence, it often interferes with the selective recovery of the valuable rare metals.​To circumvent this, the researchers borrowed from the principles of coordination chemistry and built an extremely porous membrane.​The approach uses metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), which are highly porous, sponge-like materials made by linking metal atoms with organic molecules. Scientists then chemically modified the walls of the tiny internal pores to improve performance.​In the experiments, the a water-stable MOF was modified with an organic ligand, Phosphono Methyl Imino Diacetic Acid (PMIDA).​Inside the MOF’s tiny pores, PMIDA acts like a chemical hook, strongly binding positively charged rare earth ions. The team tested the capture of three rare metals, namely neodymium, gadolinium, and dysprosium, using the ultra-porous material.At the highest ligand concentration, PMIDA captured up to 160 milligrams of neodymium, 175 milligrams of gadolinium, and 195 milligrams of dysprosium per gram of material. These recovery capacities were at least twice as high as previously reported amounts using a similar approach.Increasing the PMIDA ligand amount boosted the material’s overall performance by changing the available binding sites. Further, simulations revealed that adding extra ligand allowed the binding groups to cluster around individual rare earth ions within the pores. This arrangement formed stronger and more stable complexes to enhance capacity and structural stability.​​”What was especially interesting was that we could see not just whether the material captured the rare earths but why,” Liu said. “By combining experiments with molecular simulations, we could look inside the pores and see how changing the number of ligands changes the way these ions are held.”Selective capture, simple release​Another important finding was the ability of the material to capture the rare earth metals selectively and efficiently in the presence of unwanted materials, such as iron. The study reported minimal changes in the uptake of rare earth, even when iron was present at 100 times the concentration of the rare earth elements in the waste liquid.In one test, rare earth uptake was only about 0.3% lower than it was without iron present. ​Besides the capturing technology, the researchers also examined the release of the trace elements. A mild treatment with dilute hydrochloric acid easily extracted the trace elements, allowing the valuable material to be reused.​It is just a beginning. And further research is needed to improve the material’s selectivity, durability, and regeneration during extraction. However, the team remains optimistic about MOFs, which could provide a more sustainable replacement for the liquid-liquid solvent extraction methods used to recover rare earth elements.​The research was published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces.

title: Onkalo to bury nuclear fuel waste underground for 100,000 years
content: The Finnish Government has granted Posiva Oy an operating license for the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel. Located in Eurajoki, Finland, the facility will encapsulate and permanently dispose of nuclear waste more than 400 meters (1,312 feet) deep into 1.9-billion-year-old crystalline bedrock.This infrastructure combines an above-ground encapsulation plant with a subterranean repository, known as Onkalo. The disposal canisters designed for this repository use a structure designed to keep radioactive spent fuel completely isolated for over 100,000 years.The approval could move nuclear power’s biggest challenge out of temporary surface tanks and seal it thousands of feet underground forever.“Finland’s strong safety culture underpins the production of clean energy. It is our responsibility across generations to ensure the safe and responsible use of nuclear power, from construction through to the final disposal of spent fuel. As a result of more than 40 years of systematic efforts, Finland will launch the first final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel in the world,” said Minister of Climate and the Environment Sari Multala.Into the bedrockEver since the first nuclear plants emerged in the 1950s, nations have struggled to manage dangerous radioactive byproducts. Today, the vast majority of this hazardous waste remains locked in temporary storage facilities across the globe.The new project could provide a solution. Carved into 1.9-billion-year-old crystalline rock in southwestern Finland, Onkalo (meaning “cave” in Finnish) stretches more than 400 meters underground. To ensure safety, the facility uses a multi-barrier defense system to isolate the waste permanently. Spent fuel rods from the Olkiluoto and Loviisa plants are sealed inside thick, corrosion-resistant copper canisters. Workers then lower these containers into bedrock shafts, surrounding them with swellable bentonite clay to absorb moisture and block movement. Finally, massive steel-reinforced concrete plugs seal the subterranean tunnels shut.The site is designed to hold up to 6,500 tonnes (7,200 tons) of uranium waste, which equals roughly 3,300 canisters. Once operations are fully underway, workers will bury up to 60 canisters per year.By the 2120s, the entire labyrinth will be completely backfilled, sealed, and handed over to the state. The surface will be quiet once more.Built over 22 yearsThe green light follows a crucial safety assessment issued on 4 August 2026 by Finland’s Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (STUK).The project has reached several key regulatory milestones on its path to full operation. Radiation safety authorities approved the initial STUK evaluation in August 2026, paving the way for the government to grant an operating license valid through 2070. Final commissioning and testing are currently underway at the facility. Commercial operations will begin once STUK completes its pending pre-operational inspection on a date yet to be determined.The Finnish firm Posiva will also need to submit periodic safety assessments every decade.The $1.16 billion project has been in the works for 22 years. The waste will remain radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After 100,000 years, radiation levels will decay back to those of natural uranium ore.While countries like Sweden and France are pursuing similar deep geological repositories, Finland has officially crossed the finish line first.Sweden is building its own deep geological repository at Forsmark, making it the second nation to begin constructing a permanent facility for spent nuclear fuel. The facility depends on the same KBS-3 isolation technology pioneered alongside Finland. It will encase high-level radioactive waste in durable copper canisters surrounded by swellable bentonite clay.

title: 1,700-TEU electric ship design wins approval for 151 MWh battery power
content: A container ship designed to carry 1,700 TEU could move regional cargo using battery power without producing direct carbon emissions during operation.Hanwha Power announced on October 23 that the concept had received Approval in Principle (AiP) from the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS).The fully electric design combines a 151 MWh energy storage system with containerized batteries and port charging infrastructure. It targets short-sea and regional container transport, with battery units that can be handled and stowed like standard freight containers.The AiP certificate was presented on October 22 at the Maritime Hybrid, Electric & Hydrogen Fuel Cells Conference & Exhibition in Bergen, Norway. Jong-kyu Hwang, Hanwha Power’s Vice President of Technology Solutions, attended alongside senior ABS representatives.Batteries take on the propulsion roleElectrical energy stored in the containerized battery units serves as the vessel’s primary propulsion source. Charging infrastructure at ports would supply the electricity needed for operation, allowing the concept to avoid direct carbon emissions while sailing.The 151 MWh system is central to the design, bringing large-scale battery storage into a containership intended for regional routes. The announcement describes a vessel concept that has received approval in principle; it does not announce the delivery or entry into service of a completed ship.Hanwha Power said the approval strengthens its capabilities in fully electric vessel design and broadens its marine propulsion portfolio. The company plans to use the development to pursue opportunities in the next-generation zero-carbon maritime transport market.Containerized units support flexible replacementThe batteries’ containerized format allows them to be handled and stowed in the same manner as standard cargo containers. According to Hanwha Power, this arrangement improves space efficiency, maximizes cargo capacity, and optimizes overall vessel performance.The approach also supports flexible battery replacement and scalable operation. Hanwha Power presented these features as a practical pathway toward reducing emissions from short-sea and regional container transport.The concept brings electric propulsion and battery storage together as an integrated solution. Its operation without direct carbon emissions depends on electricity stored onboard and the use of charging infrastructure in port.The release did not specify the vessel’s operating range, charging time, service speed, or construction schedule. Those details were not included in the description of the newly approved design.Smaller electric vessel design also completedAlongside the 1,700-TEU concept, Hanwha Power has completed the basic design of a 1,000-TEU battery-powered container vessel. The company aims to develop a wider lineup of electric-propulsion ships suited to different operating conditions and customer requirements.“This AiP from ABS marks an important step in extending Hanwha Power’s marine technology capabilities to fully electric vessels powered by large-scale battery systems,” said Jong-kyu Hwang.“We will address the needs of the next-generation zero-carbon maritime transport market with integrated solutions that combine electric propulsion and containerized battery system technologies,” he added. Together, the two designs support Hanwha Power’s effort to expand its electric vessel portfolio, with the larger concept now holding ABS Approval in Principle.

title: Genetically modified dogs could bring sharper senses to military K-9s
content: A startup backed by de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences wants to change how the U.S. military sources its working dogs. Warhound has emerged from stealth with $200 million in funding and a $1.2 billion valuation. Its plan involves genetically engineering dogs for dangerous missions, including explosives detection and specialized search operations.Colossal CEO Ben Lamm founded the venture with Palmer Luckey, co-founder of defense technology company Anduril. Warhound aims to combine genetic engineering with protective equipment and digital systems designed to support dogs and their human handlers.The company enters a specialized market with a domestic supply problem. Warhound says more than 80% of working dogs used by the U.S. military come from Europe. It also claims fewer than half of those dogs qualify for service.Engineering better working dogsWarhound plans to start with two breeds already valued for military and police work. Belgian Malinois and German Shepherds will provide the cell lines for its genetic engineering program.Researchers will store those cell lines in a biobank before modifying the dogs’ genetic makeup. The goal is to improve traits linked to mission performance and reduce inherited health risks.Lamm told TechCrunch that conventional breeding can produce dogs with poor eyesight or genetic predispositions to cancer. Hip dysplasia and muscle atrophy can also prevent animals from completing training.Warhound wants to improve canine health and longevity alongside traits such as speed, agility, and scent detection. Enhanced olfactory capabilities could prove particularly useful during explosives searches.The approach builds on Colossal’s existing work in genetic engineering and animal cloning. The company has pursued efforts to recreate extinct species, including the dodo and woolly mammoth. Its biotechnology could now serve a more immediate military application.Anduril adds protective technologyGenetics represents only one part of Warhound’s plan. Anduril will contribute hardware and software designed to improve protection and coordination during missions.Potential equipment includes protective vests and goggles for working dogs. Lamm also described sensor-equipped vests that could relay information to handlers, giving them a clearer picture of conditions in the field.The goal, he said, is to make dogs safer, healthier, and more capable in service. Anduril’s technology will focus on equipment worn by the animals, not genetic modifications.The funding round includes investors such as In-Q-Tel, Sequoia, and 8VC. Luckey serves as a partner in the venture but does not hold equity in Warhound, according to Lamm. Colossal owns a stake and licenses its technology to the startup.First dogs expected in 2027Warhound expects its first cloned dogs to arrive early next year. Colossal-owned cloning company ViaGen will help produce the animals. Lamm hopes they will enter service within two years.The startup has not disclosed pricing. Its prospective customers include the Department of Defense, police departments, military organizations and emergency responders. Lamm said Warhound has briefed government groups about its business.The company is also working with the American Humane Society on certification for its training program. It hopes retired dogs will enter the society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program or another suitable placement program.Important questions remain about oversight, animal welfare, and the safe deployment of genetically modified dogs. Warhound says buyers will manage the animals under the same training framework used for military working dogs. Its first animals will show whether the proposed combination of genetic engineering and field equipment can deliver practical results.

title: 3D propeller molecules create a rare quantum lattice with edge states
content: Organic molecules have produced an electronic behavior that researchers have struggled to engineer in molecular materials. Scientists assembled triptycene-based molecules into a rare two-dimensional lattice and detected quantum states confined to its edges. The finding could widen the options for designing materials used in future electronic and quantum devices.The structure combines features of honeycomb and Kagome lattices, arrangements that scientists study for their unusual electronic properties. Its edge states also demonstrate that organic molecular assemblies can support topological behavior, an area of research dominated by inorganic materials.The findings appeared in Nano Letters on Sept. 2, 2026. The international team included researchers from Japan’s National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS), several Japanese universities, and Germany’s Kiel University.Hybrid molecular latticeThe researchers created what scientists call a diatomic Kagome lattice. Its geometry combines elements of two distinct lattice patterns.Honeycomb lattices resemble a beehive’s repeating cells. Graphene, a single layer of graphite, follows this arrangement. Kagome lattices take their name from a traditional Japanese basket-weaving pattern.Scientists have extensively investigated both structures because their geometry can produce distinctive electronic properties. However, researchers have rarely fabricated a diatomic Kagome lattice in an actual material.The team used derivatives of triptycene, a molecule whose three planes form a propeller-like arrangement. Those molecular planes make contact with neighboring structures, strengthening electronic interactions within the assembled material.That detail matters because organic molecules typically couple weakly through electronic interactions. Their structures offer considerable design flexibility, but those weak connections can make it difficult to reproduce the properties required for quantum materials.Unusual states at edgesThe team examined its molecular assembly using a scanning tunneling microscope. The measurements revealed electronic states concentrated along the structure’s boundary, where the lattice meets its surroundings.The researchers then used theoretical analysis to identify these features as topological edge states. These states emerge from the topology, or mathematical structure, of a material’s electronic properties. They occupy the edges rather than behaving like electronic states within the interior.Their presence provides evidence that the organic assembly exhibits the distinctive properties of a topological quantum material. The strong electronic coupling between neighboring triptycene derivatives helps explain how the structure supports this behavior.The result offers researchers a different way to approach quantum material design. Instead of relying primarily on inorganic compounds, scientists can investigate how molecular geometry and stronger electronic interactions create useful quantum properties.Future quantum applicationsThe team sees potential applications in electronics that consume less power and switch states rapidly. Future studies could investigate whether related structures can transition between semiconductor-like behavior and superconductivity.Researchers also envision ultra-fast optical switches and energy transport without losses at room temperature. Neither capability has been demonstrated in this experiment, and achieving them would require further research.The immediate achievement is more specific. Scientists have shown that an organic molecular assembly can host topological edge states through a deliberately engineered lattice. That gives researchers a new structure to investigate as they work to understand how molecular design can control electronic behavior.

title: GM tests 300,000 battery designs virtually, gets approval in a month
content: General Motors (GM) says it virtually tested more than 300,000 electric vehicle battery designs before building a physical prototype, helping the US automaker move from its first battery-pack concept to formal program approval in just one month.The achievement is part of GM’s development of its fourth-generation EV platform, which aims to deliver longer driving ranges, lower manufacturing costs and simpler vehicle designs.The company is using computer simulations and a new engineering approach that allows design, manufacturing and engineering teams to work simultaneously rather than completing their tasks one after another.GM expects the approach to cut its traditional five-year vehicle development timeline in half.Testing 300,000 battery designsAt the center of the new platform is lithium manganese-rich (LMR) battery technology, which GM is developing for its high-volume electric vehicles.Instead of manufacturing and physically testing hundreds of battery designs, engineers used computer models to evaluate more than 300,000 possible configurations before producing a prototype.According to GM, this helped its engineering team move from an initial LMR battery-pack concept to formal program approval in just one month.The batteries will use prismatic cells manufactured by Ultium Cells, GM’s joint venture with LG Energy Solution, in Spring Hill, Tennessee.GM says its LMR chemistry is designed to deliver 33% greater energy density than lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, a widely used lower-cost alternative.Higher energy density could allow automakers to achieve longer driving ranges without increasing battery size or weight.GM estimates that its fourth-generation EV platform, combining LMR batteries with improved electric motors and aerodynamics, could deliver roughly 20% more driving range per kilowatt-hour of energy than its current vehicles.These improvements remain targets for the upcoming platform rather than independently verified performance figures.Simplifying future electric vehiclesBeyond batteries, GM is redesigning the motors, electronics and electrical systems used in its next generation of EVs.The company says its new electric drive units contain 40% fewer parts, making them smaller and lighter while potentially reducing manufacturing costs.Its updated electrical architecture also uses 30% less wiring and fewer control modules than current GM electric vehicles.A centralized computing system is designed to provide 40 times more processing power, supporting software updates, energy management, and driver-assistance features such as Super Cruise.GM is also extending digital simulations into vehicle manufacturing.Engineers can use virtual models to examine assembly procedures, equipment placement and potential safety issues before installing production machinery.Once manufacturing begins, GM’s PlantBrAIn system will combine factory-floor information with computer models to identify ways to improve production.The automaker says similar methods have already helped its battery-pack assembly facilities process battery packs 30% faster.Future vehicles will also be able to check their electrical connections during assembly, potentially eliminating a final electrical validation step.GM has not specified when its fourth-generation EV platform will enter production. The company says the changes are intended to make electric vehicles more affordable while accelerating development and manufacturing.

title: US ally boosts naval warfare power, underwater operations' capability
content: A cutting-edge defense technology company has successfully completed the acquisition of a Canada-based company specializing in advanced autonomous underwater and remotely operated systems for the maritime domain. Israel-based Elbit Systems’ acquisition of International Submarine Engineering Ltd. is aimed at boosting underwater vehicle innovations.Underwater technologies will further strengthen maritime solutions“This acquisition marks another milestone in Elbit Systems’ strategy to expand its offerings in the naval domain,” said Bezhalel (Butzi) Machlis, President and CEO of Elbit Systems. “Combined with our existing capabilities in naval electronic warfare, autonomous systems, naval precision munitions and maritime mission systems, ISE’s underwater technologies will further strengthen our position as a global provider of comprehensive, integrated maritime solutions.”Headquartered in the Vancouver area, ISE is a high-technology company engaged in the development and manufacture of undersea vehicles, including Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) and Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), as well as computer control systems and robotics. With more than 50 years of experience in subsea robotics, ISE has delivered over 250 underwater vehicles to customers in more than 20 countries worldwide, according to a press release.Elbit Systems’ naval portfolio includes unmanned surface vessels, underwater systems, integrated command-and-control (C2) suites, electro-optical and sonar systems, communications and electronic warfare technologies. Through its subsidiaries and global centers of excellence, Elbit Systems delivers proven naval capabilities supporting missions ranging from coastal security to blue-water operations, as per the release.The addition of ISE’s underwater autonomous technologies is intended to expand Elbit Systems’ capabilities in underwater Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), Mine Counter Measures (MCM) and Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW), further strengthening the Company’s end-to-end maritime offering.Unlike remotely operated vehicles, which are typically controlled through a communications link, AUVs can undertake planned missions with varying degrees of independence. This distinction makes autonomy particularly useful where communication with a submerged platform is difficult.Expanding its naval technology portfolioISE’s established expertise in underwater vehicles, robotics and computer control systems offers Elbit Systems an opportunity to broaden the range of maritime technologies it can develop and integrate.Modern naval operations increasingly depend on the coordination of multiple platforms rather than the capabilities of a single vessel or sensor. Aircraft, surface vessels, underwater vehicles and shore-based command systems can each contribute different forms of information and operational support.Elbit Systems’ acquisition of ISE fits this wider industry trend towards integrated autonomous operations. The company’s existing maritime portfolio includes its Seagull unmanned surface vessel, while ISE adds further expertise in autonomous underwater vehicles and remotely operated systems.For Elbit Systems, the purchase of ISE represents a further step in expanding its naval technology portfolio. By adding a company with a long record in underwater robotics, Elbit gains access to specialist expertise that complements its existing surface, sensor, communications and command-and-control capabilities.

title: US firm unveils turbine core to power supersonic jets, 42MW generators
content: Boom Supersonic, a US aerospace company best known for developing the Overture supersonic passenger airliner, has unveiled its first 14,000-pound turbine core, designed to support both high-speed aircraft and natural gas power generation.The prototype, called Sprint Core, will serve as the foundation for the company’s Symphony jet engine and its Superpower 42-megawatt gas turbine.Boom said the core has been shipped from its research and development facility to a dedicated test site at the Colorado Air and Space Port. The company expects to begin operating the prototype by Thanksgiving.The announcement marks a step in Boom’s effort to apply technology originally developed for supersonic flight to electricity generation, where demand for additional power capacity is growing.Testing shared turbine technologyThe prototype contains a six-stage high-pressure compressor, a combustion system with 24 fuel nozzles and a single-stage high-pressure turbine.Its compressor uses components known as blisks, in which the blades and central disk are manufactured as a single piece. These are made from high-grade stainless steel and nickel-based alloys.The turbine also incorporates hollow superalloy blades designed to withstand high operating temperatures.Boom has equipped the prototype with nearly 1,000 sensors to monitor temperature, pressure, vibration, strain and other operating conditions. Including sensors on supporting systems, the total reaches approximately 2,000.Today's Boom announcements in 90 seconds pic.twitter.com/BoMA65K041— Blake Scholl 🛫 (@bscholl) October 22, 2026Some measurements will be collected millions of times per second, generating data that engineers can use to evaluate the design and improve future versions.The company emphasized that Sprint Core is an experimental prototype intended to gather engineering data, rather than a production-ready engine.Factory targets 2GW outputAlongside the prototype, Boom unveiled a $150 million manufacturing facility in Centennial, Colorado, spanning nearly 200,000 square feet across two buildings.The Superpower Superfactory is already producing components while construction continues. Once fully operational, it is expected to manufacture parts representing about 85% of each turbine’s mass, including blades, shafts and compressor components.Boom plans to install more than 75 large manufacturing and inspection machines and employ up to 500 workers.The company is targeting annual production of 1 GW, equivalent to 25 turbines, by 2028, rising to 2 GW or 50 turbines by 2029. First customer deliveries are planned for mid-2027.Boom also announced plans for an all-digital foundry capable of producing single-crystal turbine blades and vanes.These components are designed to withstand extreme temperatures and mechanical stress. The proposed manufacturing process would eliminate the need for conventional tooling, potentially allowing engineers to test new blade designs much faster.However, the foundry remains under development, with the first single-crystal components expected in 2027.The expansion comes as Boom seeks customers for its gas turbines following the reported cancellation of a $1.25 billion agreement with data-center developer Crusoe covering 29 turbines.Boom’s immediate challenge is to demonstrate that its shared turbine technology can perform reliably before scaling production for both electricity generation and supersonic aviation.

title: Claude finds bugs that survived trillions of software test runs
content: Anthropic says its Claude model has formally verified security properties in 123 open-source software libraries, uncovering hundreds of bugs during the process. Some flaws had escaped detection for years, despite trillions of automated test runs.The project, conducted with software verification firm Theorem, applies mathematical proofs directly to compiled machine code. Researchers say the approach could make rigorous software verification practical for a much wider range of projects.The work targets a growing security problem. Automated tools can now discover vulnerabilities in mature software, leaving developers searching for stronger ways to prevent exploitable flaws. Formal verification offers a potential answer by proving that code follows specific rules under defined conditions.Claude finds hidden bugsTraditional software testing runs programs against selected inputs to expose failures. Fuzzing tools generate large numbers of unusual inputs, but they cannot exhaust every possible combination.Anthropic used Claude to turn existing fuzz tests into mathematical specifications. The model then generated proofs showing that 239 program entry points across 123 libraries would not crash under defined conditions.The researchers worked with RISC-V assembly code, which represents instructions executed by a processor. Claude generated roughly 180 million lines of proof code, with a typical proof spanning about 600,000 lines.A separate tool called Rocq checked the proofs against their specifications. This independent verification step means developers do not need to manually inspect every line of generated proof code. Anthropic also allowed Claude to patch bugs discovered during verification. The model then generated new proofs for the updated code.Flaws survived years of testingThe process exposed vulnerabilities that conventional fuzzing might struggle to find. One library contained a counter underflow that could trigger an out-of-bounds write during decompression.The flaw required an input of roughly 20 MB with a rare arrangement of data. Another bug involved an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and more than 2 GB of memory to expose its failure.Claude also found an out-of-bounds read that depended on a particular sequence of operations involving two handles to the same file. In another case, it rediscovered a known vulnerability in the libexpat XML parser.Not every issue caused a crash. The model also identified a logic flaw that could let an application bypass a feature designed to restrict which files it could load.These findings suggest formal verification could help uncover defects that routine testing misses. The method can also establish properties that ordinary tests cannot prove across every permitted input.Proofs have important limitsAnthropic cautioned that formally verified software is not automatically bug-free. The guarantees apply only to specific properties, inputs, and assumptions described in each proof.The current work covers single-threaded, statically linked RISC-V programs running under a modeled Linux environment. Most deployed systems use other processor architectures or different software configurations.The specifications also cannot guarantee properties they do not describe. Researchers must ensure their mathematical models accurately represent real processors and operating systems.Even with these constraints, the project points toward a broader role for formal verification in software development. Anthropic expects better models and reusable proofs to reduce the cost of checking critical software components.If developers can verify widely shared libraries once and reuse those guarantees, the approach could strengthen security across many applications that depend on them.

title: Common Chemicals Trigger Alarming Changes in Human Breast Tissue Models
content:
A breast tissue organoid that has been artificially colored. Credit: The Kuperwasser Lab
Chemicals that disrupt hormones may leave a molecular “scar” that could someday help identify people at higher risk of breast cancer, research in human breast tissue models suggests.
People are typically exposed to several chemicals at once, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals that can interfere with the body’s hormones. Scientists have increasingly questioned whether these exposures contribute to breast cancer risk. Much of the evidence, however, comes from animal models or laboratory-grown cells that cannot fully reproduce the complexity of human breast tissue.
Researchers at
Tufts University School of Medicine
Boston University
investigated those effects using three-dimensional models of normal human breast tissue called organoids. Their study, published in the
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
, found that three common bisphenols, BPA, BPS, and BPF, produced relatively few changes when tested individually. When combined at very low concentrations comparable to levels detected in human blood and urine, the chemicals disrupted normal development in organoids from most of the tissue donors.
Breast development continues long after birth
The organoids were grown from breast tissue donated by 13 healthy young women. They contain multiple types of breast cells and can reproduce some aspects of human breast tissue development, allowing researchers to examine chemical exposures during that process.
“The breast also is unusual in that it undergoes major developmental changes well after birth, including during puberty and pregnancy,” said Charlotte Kuperwasser, the study’s senior author and a professor of developmental, molecular, and chemical biology at Tufts University School of Medicine. “And the concern is that breast tissue cells may be highly sensitive to environmental cues, such as chemical exposure, during critical windows of mammary gland development.”
As the organoids developed over about three weeks, the team exposed them to individual chemicals and mixtures. The panel included substances that disrupt hormones, chemicals that affect metabolism, and known or suspected carcinogens. Researchers then analyzed changes in gene activity and DNA modifications. Different chemicals affected development in different ways, with the bisphenol mixture producing the most striking finding.
“We intentionally used concentrations of chemicals that were relevant to real-world exposure rather than the very high doses sometimes used in toxicology studies,” said Kuperwasser. “We also tested a mixture of these because people are typically exposed to multiple chemicals at the same time.”
A molecular resemblance to lobular cancer
To explore how the changes associated with the bisphenol mixture might relate to disease, the team compared them with molecular data from human breast cancers. The exposure-associated pattern was most strongly represented in data from patients with invasive lobular carcinoma, a type of breast cancer that may not produce a detectable lump and can be difficult to detect with a mammogram.
That resemblance does not establish that the chemicals cause cancer or explain how the observed changes might contribute to breast disease. The researchers instead describe the work as a new way to investigate how environmental exposures affect normal human tissue before cancer develops.
“Historically, we have thought about cancer risk largely in terms of inherited mutations, lifestyle factors, and exposures that directly damage DNA,” said Kuperwasser. “These findings raise another possibility: Environmental exposures may subtly alter how normal tissues develop, leaving behind molecular changes that do not cause cancer by themselves but may make the tissue more permissive to cancer many years later.”
Molecular “scars” might guide earlier screening
Kuperwasser noted that persistent molecular changes could eventually serve as a biological record, like a “scar” of past exposure. If validated in people, such markers could potentially help identify individuals at higher risk of breast cancer and guide earlier or more targeted screening.
“If these results are validated by additional studies, they could change how we think about cancer prevention,” said Kuperwasser.
Studies involving larger and more diverse groups of donors, along with a broader range of chemicals and mixtures, are needed to determine how widely the findings apply. Researchers also need to establish whether the molecular changes seen in organoids persist in human tissues and whether they are associated with, or contribute to, breast disease later in life.

title: A Deadly Virus Has Been Hiding in Brazil for 142 Years – and Scientists Just Uncovered a Hidden Danger
content:
Sabiá virus is a rare, potentially deadly pathogen first identified in Brazil in 1990. It belongs to the arenavirus family and can cause severe hemorrhagic fever, with symptoms that may include bleeding, neurological complications, and organ dysfunction. Credit: Stock
Scientists have uncovered new clues about the evolution of a rare, deadly Brazilian virus that has circulated largely undetected for more than a century.
A rare and deadly virus went undetected in Brazil after genetic changes allowed it to escape existing laboratory tests. Scientists investigating two fatal infections have now identified the mutations responsible, developed an improved detection method, and uncovered evidence that the pathogen has circulated in the country for more than a century.
The Sabiá virus can cause severe hemorrhagic and neurological illness, yet only four fatal cases have been documented in São Paulo state since 1990. New genomic research, published in
PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases
, suggests that additional infections may have escaped diagnosis.
Why Existing Tests Failed to Detect the Virus
The investigation focused on two infections identified in 2019 and 2020. Researchers recovered viral genomes that were approximately 89% genetically identical to strains described in 1999. Crucially, some mutations affected the regions recognized by the DNA primers used in diagnostic tests, preventing those tests from detecting the circulating virus.
“The reference strain of the Sabiá virus dates back to 1990, from a case in Cotia. The diagnostic method was developed based on that genome. Since more than 30 years have passed, it was very likely that the virus had mutated. We don’t have enough cases to validate this method further, but it can be used for future suspected cases with greater accuracy than the tests used until now,” says Ingra Morales Claro, who conducted the research during her doctoral studies at the University of São Paulo Medical School (FM-USP) with a FAPESP scholarship. She is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Kentucky.
“When analyzing the genomes of the new cases, we identified mutations in target regions of the primers that prevented detection by existing diagnostic tests. We modified those regions, and now it’s possible to identify the circulating strains,” Claro explains. The redesigned primers have been sent to the Adolpho Lutz Institute, a major public health laboratory in São Paulo.
Two Fatal Infections Uncovered Through Genetic Analysis
One case involved a 52-year-old man from Sorocaba who had a history of hiking in forested areas. He sought medical attention on December 30, 2019, and was transferred to the Hospital das Clínicas (Hospital das Clínicas) in São Paulo with suspected yellow fever. Initial tests for yellow fever and Sabiá virus were negative, and he died on January 11, 2020.
Researchers eventually detected Sabiá virus in his blood using metagenomic analysis, which searches for genetic material from multiple microorganisms without requiring scientists to identify a particular pathogen in advance. The rapid approach had been developed during Claro’s doctoral research to detect emerging pathogens in clinical samples.
The discovery prompted the team to examine blood samples from seven earlier patients with acute hemorrhagic and neurological illness who had tested negative for yellow fever. One sample revealed another Sabiá infection in a 63-year-old rural worker from Assis. He had been admitted to the Hospital das Clínicas on December 10, 2019, and died two days later.
Genetic Evidence Points to a Much Older Virus
Analysis of the newly recovered genomes identified changes in a viral protein involved in binding to human cells. Although these alterations could be relevant to how the virus interacts with its hosts, the study did not establish whether they changed its ability to infect people or cause severe disease.
The researchers also reconstructed the virus’s evolutionary history using phylogenetic analysis, which compares genetic differences to estimate relationships between viral lineages. Their findings suggest that Sabiá has been circulating in Brazil for approximately 142 years, rather than representing a recent introduction.
“There were likely other cases in the past that went unidentified. It’s important to understand the virus, develop tests, and study the changes occurring in its genome so that we can anticipate future cases, and even outbreaks, of the disease,” warns Ester Sabino, a professor at FM-USP who coordinates the Brazil-UK Joint Center for Arbovirus Discovery, Diagnostics, Genomics, and Epidemiology (CADDE) in Brazil.
The Unknown Animal Reservoir
Scientists have not established which animal species naturally maintains Sabiá virus, although wild rodents are considered possible reservoirs. The known infections occurred in rural settings where people may encounter wildlife, but the precise route of transmission remains uncertain.
The investigation was carried out by CADDE researchers affiliated with FM-USP and Imperial College London, with
support from FAPESP
. The center has also contributed to genomic investigations of SARS-CoV-2, Zika, mpox, and yellow fever. Sabino helped lead Brazil’s first sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 in March 2020 and subsequent sequencing of mpox in 2022. Nuno Faria, who coordinates CADDE’s UK team, has worked on genomic surveillance of Zika, yellow fever, and the SARS-CoV-2 Gamma variant.
“In this context, metagenomic approaches have proven to be essential tools for detecting rare or unexpected pathogens, especially when targeted diagnostic tests fail. This strategy was fundamental in identifying both fatal cases of Sabiá in humans and in wild animals, and it highlights the essential role of genomic surveillance in detecting public health risks,” says Faria, referring also to the group’s
research
on yellow fever evolution and transmission in Brazil.
A Major Challenge for Future Research
Studying Sabiá virus presents unusual laboratory safety challenges. It is considered one of the Brazilian viruses with the greatest risk of transmission through infectious aerosols in laboratory settings. Handling the active virus requires the highest level of biosafety containment, which is not currently available in South America.
Brazil plans to address that limitation with Orion, a laboratory being built at the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM) in Campinas. Scheduled to open in 2030, it will be the country’s first facility equipped to store and handle active Sabiá virus. The reference strain is currently held in the United States.

title: MIT Scientists Reprogram Immune Cells Inside the Body To Destroy Cancer
content:
Targeted lipid nanoparticles (blue) deliver mRNA to NK cells inside the body. Credit: MIT
Natural killer cells reprogrammed inside mice eliminated lymphoma tumors and helped damaged livers heal, though whether this approach could help people with cancer or autoimmune disease remains unknown.
To make a cancer treatment from a patient’s T cells, doctors first collect a blood sample and send it to a laboratory. There, these immune cells are isolated and engineered to carry chimeric antigen receptors, or CARs, proteins that recognize a chosen target, such as a cancer protein. Once enough modified cells have been produced, they are shipped back to the hospital and infused into the patient. When a CAR detects its target, it activates the T cell to destroy the cell carrying it.
Producing similar treatments from natural killer (NK) cells poses many of the same manufacturing challenges, adding time and expense. MIT engineers have now developed a way to reprogram NK cells inside the body, without removing them for laboratory engineering. In experiments in mice, their approach successfully reprogrammed about 80 percent of the targeted NK cells. The study was published in
Nature Biotechnology
Over the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven CAR T-cell cancer treatments. These therapies have had considerable success against blood cancers, primarily those originating in B cells, including several types of leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma. No CAR NK-cell therapies are currently FDA-approved, although many researchers are developing them for cancer and autoimmune disorders.
Nanoparticles program NK cells inside the body
“The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells,” says Daniel Anderson, the study’s senior author, a professor in MIT’s Department of Chemical Engineering, and a member of MIT’s Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.
To deliver those instructions, the team designed lipid nanoparticles, tiny particles made from fatty molecules, that carry messenger RNA. The mRNA encodes a CAR protein that the receiving cell can make. Antibody fragments coating the particles bind to receptors on the surface of NK cells, helping direct the payload to the intended cells. This allows the engineering to happen “in vivo,” meaning inside the body.
The CAR encoded by the mRNA can be chosen according to the intended target. For example, the instructions could produce a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein found on T cells, including autoreactive T cells that mistakenly attack the body’s own tissues.
“If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs,” Anderson says.
When T cells attack each other
Using NK cells also addresses a difficulty that arises when engineered T cells are used against T-cell diseases. A CAR designed to recognize T-cell proteins may lead the engineered T cells to kill one another along with the diseased cells. NK cells can target T cells without that problem.
“NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies — not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases,” says MIT postdoc Yuang Chen, who is a lead author of the study alongside MIT graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal.
Targeted lipid nanoparticles (teal) deliver mRNA (coral) to NK cells (orange) to enable tumor targeting; blue structures depict surface proteins, the pink cell represents a tumor cell, and red discs are red blood cells. Credit: MIT
Tumor clearance and liver healing in mice
The researchers tested the approach against T-cell lymphoma in humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them a human-like immune system. After five injections of the reprogramming nanoparticles, the tumors were eradicated. The result was similar to treatment with CAR NK cells made through the conventional process of removing NK cells, reprogramming them outside the body, and returning them to the mice.
The same delivery strategy could also equip NK cells to attack autoreactive T cells. To test that possibility, the team studied mice with autoimmune hepatitis, in which T cells attack liver cells called hepatocytes. After a single injection of the nanoparticles, the autoreactive T cells were destroyed, and liver damage healed.
The experiments also extended beyond diseases involving dysfunctional T cells. In a mouse model of an aggressive form of melanoma, three of five mice went into complete remission after receiving nanoparticles that reprogrammed their NK cells to target the cancer cells.
“This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases,” says study coauthor Robert Langer, the David H. Koch Institute Professor at MIT.
The researchers hope that engineered NK cells could eventually be used to treat other autoimmune disorders caused by dysfunctional T cells, including multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Anderson, 13 October 2026,
Nature Biotechnology
DOI: 10.1038/s41587-026-03310-1

title: Scientists Discover Ancient Human DNA Hidden in Cave Walls for Thousands of Years
content:
Pigment sampling at a claviform rock art figure in Tebellín, Spain. Credit: Alberto Martínez Villa
Ancient DNA from cave walls offers clues to prehistoric visitors’ sex and ancestry, potentially allowing scientists to investigate who used these spaces without disturbing archaeological deposits.
A cave wall can hold traces of prehistoric visitors even when it has no paintings or other visible signs of human activity. Scientists have recovered ancient human DNA from cave walls for the first time, showing that genetic material can survive on these surfaces for thousands of years. Several positive results came from unpainted areas that researchers had sampled as negative controls.
The search began with an interest in the people who made prehistoric art. The interdisciplinary First Art project aims to date the earliest cave art and characterize its chemical composition. Led by researchers from Spain and Portugal, it involves institutions across those countries, the UK, China, and Germany. Collaboration with researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology extended that work to DNA analysis, taking the search for ancient genetic material beyond bones, sediments, and, more recently, bone artifacts.
“We know that some of the art was applied to cave walls by blowing or rubbing pigment onto the surface. Given the enormous sensitivity of current ancient DNA analysis techniques, we were eager to see if this type of contact could leave traces of DNA in the rock art, potentially allowing us to obtain genetic profiles from the makers of the art,” says Hipólito Collado Giraldo, an archaeologist and rock art specialist from the Extremadura Government in Spain, who brought together the First Art team.
Polychrome ceiling of Altamira from which pigment samples were analyzed. Credit: Matthias Meyer
Unpainted walls hold ancient human DNA
The researchers examined 24 rock art panels from 11 caves, including simple marks and hand stencils, along with pigment that had naturally fallen from figurative paintings in the famous Cave of Altamira. Using advanced DNA extraction and sequencing methods, they analyzed pigmented and unpigmented cave wall fragments, sediments, bones, and a rare prehistoric bird bone airbrush used to blow red ochre onto cave walls.
Of the 54 samples collected, only five yielded authentic ancient human mitochondrial DNA, genetic material found in the energy-producing structures inside cells. One came from a calcite crust with pigment underneath it on Panel 11 in Escoural Cave, Portugal. Two came from unpigmented walls in a deeper gallery of the same cave, and two others came from unpigmented surfaces beside rock art in Covarón Cave in northern Spain. The unpigmented areas had initially been sampled as negative controls, making their positive results unexpected.
Two of the five samples contained no detectable mitochondrial DNA from other animals. That rare pattern strongly suggests that humans deposited the DNA directly, through saliva or other bodily fluids. The other three positive samples, all from unpigmented walls, contained both human and animal DNA. This mixture suggests an indirect route, likely involving sediment transfer or water movement carrying genetic material onto the surfaces.
“Although we cannot directly connect the traces of ancient human DNA we have found to the creation of rock art, this is the first evidence for human DNA preservation on cave walls for thousands of years,” says first author Alba Bossoms Mesa, a doctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. “It is exciting to think that we may have uncovered a new way to study prehistoric human presence.”
DNA links cave visitors to hunter-gatherers
The recovered DNA nevertheless provided information about some of the people who had been in the caves. Human DNA in three samples came mostly from females, while one sample contained DNA mostly from males. The fifth remained undetermined. Further analysis of the two unpigmented samples from Covarón showed that their DNA came from modern humans, or Homo sapiens. Nuclear DNA, the genetic material housed in cell nuclei, placed them within the Western hunter-gatherer genetic cluster, consistent with findings for other ancient Iberian populations.
Calcite fragment with pigment underneath from Escoural, Portugal, stored in a membrane box. Credit: Alba Bossoms Mesa
“This study fundamentally changes how we think about where ancient DNA can be found,” says senior author Matthias Meyer, a paleogeneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology who co-led the work with Collado Giraldo. “We were surprised to see that ancient DNA can be recovered not only from pigmented samples, but also from cave walls that show no visible evidence of past human activity. We can now ask new questions: Who touched this wall? Was it a man or a woman? Which population did they belong to? How far did ancient humans venture into deep cave systems?”
Sampling cave walls could offer a way to investigate prehistoric human behavior without disturbing archaeological deposits. Genetic evidence from these surfaces could help researchers establish the biological sex and ancestry of people who used caves, even where their activities left no recognizable images or objects.
“This is not just about rock art,” says Collado Giraldo. “It’s about understanding how people used caves and where they left their marks.”
The cave artists remain unidentified
Recovering that evidence remains difficult, even from an object expected to have been in contact with saliva. The bird bone airbrush from Altamira yielded no ancient human DNA. The most likely explanation was extremely high contamination by present-day human DNA, combined with the minimal amount of material sampled. The result highlights the difficulty of recovering ancient genetic traces from material that has been heavily handled over decades of study.
Despite favorable preservation conditions at many sites, ancient DNA was detected in only one of the 24 rock art panels examined and in two additional locations adjacent to other panels. That rarity suggests pigment surfaces seldom retain enough DNA to survive for thousands of years, particularly without protection from mineral crusts or sealed environments.
“The preservation of human DNA on cave walls is highly variable,” says Bossoms Mesa. “But when it does survive, it tells a powerful story. And while these first results are promising, I think our priority now should be to refine the methods and to understand under what conditions we can expect a higher success rate.”
Identifying the makers of particular artworks remains a possibility for future research, rather than something this study has achieved.
“This is just the beginning,” adds Meyer. “We now know that cave walls are archives of past human presence. The next step is to test more sites, art styles and techniques, especially hand stencils and figurative art in caves with good molecular preservation, as far as minimally invasive sampling allows.”

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Oxygen Source Deep Inside Earth That Could Rewrite Our Planet’s History
content:
Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way magma stores oxygen within its structure. The discovery could reshape our understanding of ancient volcanic activity and planetary atmospheres. Credit: Shutterstock
Ancient eruptions may have helped shape the air we breathe, with laboratory experiments revealing magma’s unexpected ability to store extra oxygen.
Molten rock deep inside Earth can take up an extra supply of oxygen under pressure, according to a new study. That finding raises the possibility that rising magma could release oxygen on its way to the surface, a process that may have contributed to increases in atmospheric oxygen billions of years ago.
Oxygen makes up more than half the atoms in Earth’s silicate interior, but its abundance does not necessarily mean it is available to escape into the atmosphere. Much of it is chemically bound to other elements. Geoscientists have generally assumed that the quantities and electrical charge states of elements such as silicon, magnesium, and iron determine how much oxygen magma contains. Knowing those ingredients should let them calculate the oxygen needed to balance the chemistry. Whether molten rock could absorb additional oxygen as a separate volatile component, as it does water and carbon dioxide, has remained largely unexplored.
The study, published in
National Science Review
, was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR). They worked with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
Pressure boosts magma’s oxygen uptake
To test whether magma could take up oxygen beyond that calculated amount, the researchers needed to give it an additional oxygen supply. They added platinum oxide (PtO₂) to create an oxygen-rich environment for synthetic mid-ocean ridge basalt, a laboratory-made version of volcanic rock from the ocean floor. Using piston-cylinder and cubic presses, they melted the basalt at temperatures of 1,200 to 1,800 °C (about 2,190 to 3,270 °F) and pressures ranging from 1 atmosphere to 7 gigapascals. At the upper end, that pressure is roughly 1 million pounds per square inch.
The team also ran experiments at the same pressures and temperatures without platinum oxide. Comparing the two sets would help reveal whether making extra oxygen available changed how much the molten rock retained.
Excess oxygen in silicate glass increases with pressure. Circles and diamonds show experiments on basalt that was fully molten or partly molten, respectively; open symbols mark control runs without an added oxygen source; squares show molecular dynamics results for MgSiO3 melt. Colors indicate temperature. The dashed line marks the starting composition. Credit: Science China Press
After rapidly cooling, or quenching, the melts into glass, the researchers measured the oxygen remaining in each sample. Not all of it counted as extra. Some was needed to balance the other elements, and some was contained in water and carbon dioxide. By measuring the glass’s elemental composition and its water and carbon dioxide contents, the team could subtract those accounted-for amounts from the total oxygen. They called the remainder “excess oxygen.”
With platinum oxide added, excess oxygen was close to zero at 1 atmosphere but exceeded 5% of the sample’s weight at 7 gigapascals. The control experiments without platinum oxide yielded only 0.2% to 0.5% excess oxygen by weight. High pressure therefore appeared to help the melt take advantage of the additional oxygen supply. Some oxygen may have escaped during quenching, so the measured amounts likely underestimate how much the molten samples originally held.
Oxygen becomes part of the glass
There was another distinction to resolve: had the oxygen become part of the material, or was it simply trapped inside gas bubbles? Raman spectroscopy, which uses scattered light to probe a material’s structure, detected no signature of oxygen gas in the glass. That indicated the excess oxygen had been incorporated into the glass structure.
Simulations led by Niu examined how the melt could accommodate this extra oxygen at the atomic level. The team used deep neural network (DNN) interatomic potentials, computational models that describe how atoms interact, with the accuracy of
ab initio
calculations based on fundamental physical principles. In the simulations, oxygen entered the melt until equilibrium was reached, meaning there was no further net uptake.
Schematic cross-section of Earth’s mantle. Magma formed in a deep, oxygen-rich region of the mantle carries excess oxygen upward. As the magma rises and pressure drops, excess oxygen is released (blue dots), which could oxidize the shallow mantle, the crust, and the atmosphere. LIP: large igneous province; ULVZ: ultra-low velocity zone. Credit: Science China Press
As more oxygen dissolved, the electrical charges on oxygen atoms spread across a wider range, and a small fraction of those atoms formed peroxide-like bonds with one another. These changes offered clues to how the melt’s chemistry could accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by the conventional accounting. The simulations used a simplified magnesium-silicon-oxygen system and produced lower oxygen contents than the basalt experiments, but they reproduced the same increase with pressure.
That pressure dependence resembles the behavior of water and carbon dioxide, which dissolve more readily in magma at higher pressures. The authors therefore suggest that oxygen should also be treated as a separate component of silicate melts. Doing so could change how researchers assess the evolution of magma oceans, the release of volatile substances, and the development of planetary atmospheres, with implications for long-term habitability on other terrestrial planets.
Magma may have supplied atmospheric oxygen
Within Earth, magma formed in oxidized regions of the mantle could collect substantial excess oxygen while under pressure. As it rises, the falling pressure could reduce how much oxygen it can retain, causing a gradual release. The oxygen could then drive oxidation reactions in the shallow mantle, crust, and atmosphere, allowing magma to transport oxidizing power from deep underground toward the surface.
The researchers propose that this process may help explain a timing overlap in Earth’s history. Major increases in atmospheric oxygen roughly 2.5 to 2.0 billion years ago coincided with the formation of some of the largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), vast accumulations of rock produced by volcanic activity. Their rough estimate suggests that if magma erupted during that period released just 0.27% of its weight as excess oxygen, it could have supplied as much oxygen as today’s atmosphere contains.
Reference: “Magma as a carrier of non-stoichiometric oxygen linking Earth’s interior and atmosphere” by Yongjiang Xu, Haiyang Niu, Wim van Westrenen, Ruiheng Liu, Peiyan Wu, Ho-Kwang Mao and Yanhao Lin, 25 August 2026,

title: What if Dark Energy Was Once Negative? Scientists Uncover a Surprising New Possibility
content:
Dark energy is a mysterious force believed to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe. Thought to make up roughly 70% of the cosmos, its true nature remains one of the biggest mysteries in modern physics. Credit: Stock
A gravity model that lets dark energy change sign could help resolve a persistent disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding.
In an existing theory of gravity, the same present-day matter density can fit two very different histories of the universe. Researchers had largely pursued the one that kept dark energy’s density positive. Exploring the other has now revealed a possible history in which that density began below zero and turned positive billions of years later.
Dark energy is the mysterious ingredient believed to drive the universe’s accelerating expansion. The simplest explanation treats it as unchanged throughout cosmic history. In the new analysis, however, the effects attributed to dark energy arise from a modified description of gravity. Its density is an effective quantity derived from the gravitational equations, rather than a property of a newly introduced substance.
Prof. Özgür Akarsu of Istanbul Technical University’s (ITU) Department of Physics led the international study, published in 2025 in
Physical Review D
. The work was carried out in his ITU research group with postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. They collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, a former postdoctoral researcher in the group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University’s Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, one of the world’s leading centers for theoretical physics.
A possible solution to the Hubble tension
Akarsu and collaborators had already been developing a scenario called sign-switching ΛCDM, or ΛsCDM. In that scenario, the cosmological constant switches from negative to positive a few billion years after the Big Bang. Analyses have shown that this history can agree with observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and ease several long-standing disagreements in cosmology. Among them is the Hubble tension, the mismatch between estimates of how fast the universe is expanding today.
The new gravity model offers a possible physical basis for that earlier scenario. It also shows preliminary promise in addressing the expansion-rate disagreement. In an extended version that includes a cosmological constant, the model remains consistent with the cosmic microwave background, the ancient light left over from the early universe, while accommodating the higher expansion rates measured locally.
Four cosmic histories show how dark energy may evolve. Unlike the standard model (grey) and conventional f(T) gravity (orange), a newly explored branch (blue) predicts that dark energy switched from negative to positive about 9.5 billion years ago. An extended model (dashed blue) suggests cosmic acceleration may have stopped roughly 1 billion years ago. Triangles mark the onset of acceleration. Credit: Istanbul Technical University, adapted from Akarsu et al., Phys. Rev. D 112, 083532 (2025).
That extension allows another possibility: the acceleration of cosmic expansion could have slowed, or even stopped, in the very recent past. Recent analyses of DESI data have raised this possibility as well, although the model still needs rigorous testing against the full observations.
Akarsu said, “For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI’s. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself.”
Gravity equations let dark energy change sign
The team’s starting point was teleparallel
gravity. Whereas Einstein’s general relativity describes gravity through the curvature of spacetime, teleparallel gravity uses torsion, a different geometric property associated with twisting. Researchers have investigated extensions of this approach for years to see whether modified gravity could account for cosmic acceleration.
The exponential version examined in the study contains the two mathematical branches that lead to different cosmic histories. Earlier cosmological studies had favored the branch that followed the usual expectation, inherited from general relativity, of a positive dark energy density. Its evolution closely resembles the standard cosmological model.
On the alternative branch, effective dark energy density is negative during the universe’s first few billion years. It crosses zero at a redshift of around 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, and remains positive afterward. The value governing the branch depends on the universe’s present matter density, so this behavior does not require an extra independently adjustable cosmological parameter. The basic model has six cosmological parameters, the same number as the standard ΛCDM model.
A modified theory must also account for the precise measurements that already support Einstein’s description of gravity. The paper finds that the alternative branch can remain consistent with Solar System tests because its departures from general relativity are naturally suppressed in dense environments.
Galaxy maps test whether dark energy changes
On cosmic scales, those departures provide opportunities to test the model. Alongside its predictions for expansion, researchers can examine how galaxies and larger structures grow and how gravity bends light through weak gravitational lensing. Galaxy motions offer another test through redshift-space distortions, patterns produced when those motions affect the redshifts used to map galaxy positions. Together, these measurements can help determine whether the proposed cosmic history is plausible.
DESI is making such comparisons increasingly demanding. By measuring the positions of millions of galaxies and quasars, it is assembling the largest three-dimensional map of the universe and tracing expansion over billions of years. In March 2025, the collaboration released results from its first three years of observations. When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak lensing, they strengthened earlier hints that dark energy might evolve rather than behave as a simple cosmological constant.
The strength of those hints varies with the datasets used, and they have not reached the level required for a definitive discovery. They also do not establish that dark energy changed sign. The ITU-led study was first submitted in October 2024, months before DESI’s March 2025 announcement, and provides a theoretical explanation to investigate.
The search for physical mechanisms that could produce a sign change remains active across cosmology. The authors suggest that other modified gravity theories may also contain possibilities overlooked because researchers required effective dark energy density to stay positive.
DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. Its full dataset will offer a more rigorous test of whether the apparent evolution of dark energy persists. The ITU team has not yet compared its model with that full dataset.
“We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension,” said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.
Reference: “Unexplored regions in teleparallel $f(T)$ gravity: Sign-changing dark energy density” by Ozgur Akarsu, Bilal Bulduk, Antonio De Felice, Nihan Katırcı and N. Merve Uzun, October 19, 2025,
Physical Review D

title: Scientists Turn Major Crude Oil Problem Into an Unexpected Energy Breakthrough
content:
Technology
Simple synthetic membrane supports yield surprisingly selective separation of real crude oils at steady state. Credit: KAIST
A simple membrane uses crude oil’s own deposits to separate lighter components at room temperature, with simulations suggesting nearly one-third less energy use when paired with distillation.
Refineries heat crude oil above 350°C (662°F) to separate a mixture that supplies transportation fuels and raw materials for plastics, packaging, textiles, and other consumer products. This century-old process, called distillation, vaporizes the oil and then cools the vapor to recover different fractions. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours of energy each year, roughly the annual output of 130 gigawatt-scale nuclear power plants operating continuously.
An international research team has demonstrated a simple, inexpensive membrane that could handle part of this separation at room temperature, without heating. As crude oil flows through it, components of the oil create the narrow channels that allow the membrane to distinguish between lighter and heavier molecules.
The study, published in
, was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively’s group at Georgia Tech.
Process simulations showed that using the membrane to pretreat crude oil before conventional distillation could reduce energy consumption by 31.6%, carbon dioxide emissions by 37.6%, cooling water use by 20.7%, and operating costs by 36%. Such savings could matter beyond the refinery, since refining costs influence the prices of fuels and many everyday products. Increasing cost pressures in global petrochemical markets have also intensified demand for more efficient separation technologies.
Oil buildup creates the separation channels
Manufacturing membranes for molecularly precise separation has been challenging. Conventional designs require ultrathin surface coatings that raise costs and risk defects at scale. Instead, the team passed crude oil through bare porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer widely used in industrial membranes.
“This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation,” Koh said.
As the oil passed through the PAN membrane, heavy hydrocarbons selectively deposited on the pore walls. These deposits gradually narrowed the openings, forming separation channels smaller than 2 nanometers. Lighter fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, passed through rapidly, while heavier components were retained. The buildup known as membrane fouling, normally a cause of declining performance, became the mechanism that made selective separation possible.
The bare PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those of previously reported state-of-the-art crude oil membranes. It also maintained stable performance for 28 consecutive days.
A refinery retrofit could cut emissions
The technology could fit into existing refineries as a modular filtration unit, reducing the need for major equipment replacement and making adoption easier. Lively said, “One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units – the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism – dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology.”
Distillation remains one of the refining industry’s largest sources of energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. If adopted throughout Korea’s refining and petrochemical sector, the membrane technology could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 10 million metric tons annually, equivalent to the emissions of roughly four million internal combustion vehicles.
Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study’s co-first authors, said, “Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality.”
For waste plastics, a proposed application is purifying pyrolysis oil, the oil obtained by breaking down plastics with heat. Other possible uses include recovering solvents used in battery manufacturing and pharmaceutical purification. These remain potential applications of the membrane platform.
Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, said, “By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries.”
Reference: “Crude oil fractionation by means of mesoporous polyacrylonitrile membranes” by Jihoon Choi, Hyeokjun Seo, Minyong Lee, Woong-Chul Shin, Jaemin Choi, Keonwoo Choi, Min-Jun Jang, Sung Gap Im, Jae W. Lee, Ryan P. Lively and Dong-Yeun Koh, 24 June 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10677-3
This research was supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT of Korea through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.
