title: Ancient Skeletons Reveal a Secret Hidden in Medieval Sicily for 1,000 Years
content:
Excavation of a Roman- Byzantine-Islamic-Norman sequence at Casale San Pietro. Credit: University of York
Ancient DNA reveals medieval Sicily as a genetic melting pot, where people buried in Christian and Muslim cemeteries shared roots in North Africa, Europe, and the Mediterranean.
Sicily changed rulers repeatedly between the 5th and 15th centuries CE, passing through the hands of the Roman and Byzantine Empires, Islamic dynasties, and the Normans and Swabians.
Yet centuries of violent regime changes did not necessarily bring wholesale changes in the people living on this Mediterranean island. Ancient DNA suggests that Sicily’s genetic diversity persisted through successive conquests, pointing to some population continuity despite the political upheaval.
The research, published in
PLOS One
, analyzed ancient DNA from 111 individuals excavated at 19 archaeological sites across Sicily. Their remains spanned the Roman Age to the Late Middle Ages, allowing researchers to examine ancestry across a long stretch of the island’s history as a hub of trade and conflict.
Shared ancestry across Christian and Muslim cemeteries
Dr. Nathan Wales, from the University of York’s Department of Archaeology, said, “Contrary to some past ideas, we can see this period shouldn’t be considered to be the ‘Dark Ages,’ but rather a dynamic period with interactions and distant connections.
“From the individuals’ DNA, we see people buried in Christian and Muslim cemeteries had similar ancestries stemming from North Africa and the European and Mediterranean area.”
Those Mediterranean connections extended farther south. The genetic data also showed that people of sub-Saharan African descent lived on Sicily throughout the medieval period, suggesting a long history of ongoing migration across the Mediterranean.
Everyday Sicilians missing from written history
Dr. Aurore Monnereau led the study and completed the work as part of her PhD at the University of York’s Department of Archaeology. She said, “While historical records are important to our understanding of the past, they often leave the experiences of ‘everyday’ people in the shadows, capturing major events of the Middle Ages through the lens of their authors.
“Through the analysis of ancient DNA, our study seeks to restore some of those missing voices. By integrating aDNA with written and archaeological evidence, we show that Sicily served as a central crossroads in the highly interconnected medieval world.”
The persistence of genetic diversity challenges the idea that Sicily’s conquests involved large-scale population replacement. The researchers’ broader interpretation also considers how people of different faiths lived alongside one another during these changing regimes.
Professor Martin Carver, from the University of York’s Department of Archaeology, said, “The study has shed a new light on people who traditionally don’t appear in the historical record, showing Christians and Muslims to have largely lived in prosperous multi-faith societies until the early thirteenth century, when Sicily became part of the Holy Roman Empire.”
The researchers emphasize that data from additional archaeological sites across the Mediterranean will be needed to develop a more detailed understanding of how these populations lived and changed over time.
Reference: “Genetic histories of individuals from multi-faith medieval Sicily” by Aurore Monnereau, Paola Orecchioni, Derek Hamilton, Eleanor Joan Green, Ian Noble, Richard Hagan, Marcela Sandoval-Velasco, Alessandra Molinari, Martin Carver, Camilla F. Speller and Nathan Wales, 24 June 2026,
PLOS ONE
DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0350298

title: Scientists Discover a $10 Flood Protection Trick That Works Better Than Sandbags
content:
Technology
Laboratory experiments suggest that an inexpensive household material could outperform traditional sandbags in limiting floodwater intrusion. Credit: Shutterstock
Stacking heavy sandbags against a doorway is a familiar response to flooding, but laboratory tests suggest sealing the gaps with ordinary duct tape could keep more water out.
Could a cheap roll of duct tape help protect your home from flooding? New research suggests it could make a surprisingly big difference.
In controlled tests, correctly applied duct tape on the outside of a household door reduced water leakage by 97-98%. The findings suggest that a simple low-cost measure could substantially reduce the amount of water entering a home during a flood. This is important as one of the key lessons from flood resilience research is that the best time to protect a property is before floodwater arrives.
The UK government’s 2025
FloodReady Review
called for practical, affordable measures that help households understand their risks and to prepare for flooding. And one potential contribution to this agenda might sound unlikely, at first glance.
Duct tape is more commonly associated with household repairs than flood protection. However, tests colleagues and I conducted
at the University of Hull
demonstrated how much water can enter a property through an unprotected doorway during a flood.
Inside our laboratory, we tested modern wooden, uPVC, and composite household doors, installed by trade professionals. We captured any water that leaked through the door in a sealed enclosure behind the door, as we increased water depth in 5 cm increments to a maximum depth of 60 cm. We pumped out any water that leaked through the door and continuously measured the rate of water leakage to evaluate the performance of doors and different types of protection applied to them.
Three doors, ready for flood-testing. Credit: Stuart McLelland
When testing sandbags, we stacked 54 sandbags with plastic sheeting between the door and the sandbags. For tape, the same person applied the tape for all tests to minimize any bias. It took about 10-20 minutes to apply the tape to each door.
For unprotected doors, leakage often reached thousands of liters per hour at 60 cm water depth. Applying duct tape across the external door reduced that leakage by 97-98%. Specialist sealing tapes achieved even greater reductions.
Duct tape v sandbags
For decades, sandbags have been portrayed as the go-to emergency response to flooding. But sandbags have practical limitations. They are heavy to transport, labor-intensive to deploy, and difficult to dispose of after contact with contaminated floodwater. And of course people don’t keep a supply of sandbags ready to deploy.
Water leaking through an unprotected door in the lab tests. Credit: Stuart McLelland
In our tests, sandbags provided less effective protection against leakage through tested doorways compared to the tape-based sealing methods. Their performance varied with water depth and at their most effective, only reduced leakage by 70% compared to an unprotected door at the same water depth.
The cost difference is striking. A household may already have duct tape or be able to purchase a roll for £10 or less, while finding and deploying sandbags involves significant additional costs, transport, and effort.
Duct tape is not a substitute for professionally designed flood doors, barriers, or a property-specific flood resilience plan. It is a temporary measure that may reduce water entering through particular gaps; it cannot guarantee a dry home or prevent water entering through other routes, including walls, floors, and drains.
Better than sandbags? Credit: Stuart McLelland
Its effectiveness will depend on the condition of the door and frame, the surfaces to which the tape is applied, the quality of the seal, and flood conditions. For properties at significant flood risk, professionally assessed protection remains important. For others, low-cost temporary measures could provide an additional layer of protection, though they cannot guarantee a property will remain dry.
Resilient households think ahead. They know whether they are at risk, sign up for flood warnings, and have a plan for protecting valuables, moving vehicles, and shutting off utilities if necessary. Adding duct tape to an emergency flood kit can be another small step in that process.
The wider lesson is that flood resilience does not have to start with a major investment. A £10 roll of duct tape cannot stop a flood. But our research suggests it could help keep out some of the water entering through a doorway. And that makes it a useful part of a wider plan to be prepared before the water arrives.

title: Researchers Discover a Surprising Twist in How Our Cells Age
content:
A surprising new discovery is challenging a long-held assumption about how our cells age. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists uncover a surprising paradox in how our cells age, revealing that more cellular cleanup isn’t always better and exercise may help restore a youthful balance.
Every day, our cells must dispose of damaged proteins and other unwanted material to keep themselves functioning properly. They accomplish this through a natural recycling process called autophagy, which packages cellular waste into specialized compartments where it is broken down into smaller molecular components that can be reused.
However, a new study suggests that the relationship between aging and cellular recycling is far more complicated than previously assumed.
The scientists expanded the number of cell types in their study by transforming skin cells into induced neurons like those pictured here. Credit: Caroline Kumsta, Tatiana Moreno, Sanford Burnham Prebys
Researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute reported their findings in the journal
Aging Cell
. Rather than finding a consistent decline in autophagy with age, they discovered that recycling activity follows different patterns depending on the type of cell and whether it comes from a male or female participant. Their results also suggest that physical exercise may influence this process in humans.
“We commonly see people cite this idea that autophagy declines with age, but the actual evidence for this in humans is very thin,” said senior and corresponding author Caroline Kumsta, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.
“Interest is growing in targeting autophagy to develop new healthy aging interventions,” said Tatiana Moreno, PhD ’26, the study’s lead author and a former graduate student in Kumsta’s laboratory.
“We wanted to challenge assumptions and investigate what actually happens to autophagy during aging in healthy individuals.”
Cellular Recycling Changes Differently With Age
To investigate how autophagy behaves throughout adulthood, the scientists collected blood and skin samples from volunteers between 23 and 72 years old. All participants reported that they were free of chronic diseases. The researchers also converted some of the collected skin cells into induced neurons, allowing them to examine a third type of cell.
The team then analyzed RNA transcripts in each cell type. These transcripts are produced when genetic instructions stored in DNA are “read” as part of the process of making proteins, enzymes, and other essential cellular components. By examining the transcripts, the scientists could investigate how aging and cell type affected the activity of genes involved in autophagy.
Importantly, the researchers did not rely solely on these genetic measurements. They also directly measured how quickly cells carried out autophagy, making it possible to determine whether patterns of gene expression accurately reflected the recycling process itself.
The results challenged the conventional view that autophagy steadily weakens throughout the body as people age.
Caroline Kumsta, PhD, is an assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys. Tatiana Moreno, PhD ’26, is a former graduate student in the Kumsta lab. Credit: Sanford Burnham Prebys
“We found that autophagic activity changes were not universal throughout the body and did not follow the idea that autophagy simply declines with age,” said Kumsta. “Rather, cellular recycling rates are altered differently with age in each of the cell types, and differently by sex in each of the cell types.”
In skin cells from male participants, autophagy activity decreased with age. However, the same process remained relatively constant in skin cells from female participants. Even more unexpectedly, induced neurons derived from female participants showed increased autophagy as age advanced.
Another important finding was that changes in the expression of autophagy genes did not reliably correspond to the actual speed of cellular recycling. In other words, measuring how actively these genes were being expressed did not necessarily reveal how much recycling was taking place.
“This shows that people using static measures such as transcription levels to infer what’s happening with autophagy need to be really careful about their interpretations,” said Moreno.
More Cellular Cleanup May Not Always Be Better
The scientists also explored whether autophagy activity was related to physical health and performance at different ages. Their findings raised another unexpected possibility: Higher levels of cellular recycling may not always indicate better health, particularly later in life.
Among participants aged 70 and older, greater autophagy activity was associated with worse measures of physical function across all three cell types examined.
Higher recycling activity in blood cells was linked to poorer aerobic fitness. In skin cells, increased autophagy was associated with a higher body mass index (BMI). Meanwhile, elevated autophagy in induced neurons corresponded with weaker grip strength, lower metabolism, and a higher resting heart rate.
These relationships suggest that the significance of increased autophagy may change as people grow older. Although cellular recycling is essential for maintaining health, its activity and effects may depend on a person’s age and the particular cells involved.
“I think this is an important distinction that merits continued study, as it appears that increased autophagy flux may be good in younger people yet problematic in older people,” said Kumsta.
“Autophagy and aging are so much more nuanced than previously assumed,” said Moreno. “To better translate autophagy research discoveries into potential therapies, we really need to understand what is happening on a cell-specific level and how it is affected by sex and age.”
Gentle Exercise May Influence Aging Cells
After identifying these unexpected patterns, the researchers investigated whether exercise could alter autophagy activity in older adults.
In a small pilot experiment, five volunteers aged 77-88 participated in a gentle exercise program designed to reduce their risk of falling. The program lasted 12 weeks, and the researchers collected blood samples before and after the intervention to evaluate changes in cellular recycling.
The preliminary results suggested that exercise may lower autophagy activity in blood cells toward levels more commonly observed in younger people. These changes occurred alongside improvements in physical performance.
Although the experiment involved only five participants, the findings raise the possibility that exercise could help regulate cellular recycling in ways that support healthier aging. Larger studies will be necessary to determine whether the effects can be reproduced and how they relate to long-term health.
“It is exciting to have this exercise intervention that may have a positive effect on autophagy and healthy aging, and I’m really excited to see where that goes,” said Kumsta.
Expanding Research on Exercise and Healthy Aging
To build on these initial findings, the Kumsta laboratory received a pilot grant from the Altman Clinical and Translational Research Institute at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego).
The funding will support further investigation into how exercise affects autophagy and physical function during aging. Researchers are now conducting larger studies with additional participants and improved testing methods in collaboration with the Exercise and Physical Activity Resource Center at UC San Diego.
The work could help scientists better understand when changes in cellular recycling are beneficial and when they may signal declining health. Such knowledge may eventually inform new strategies for promoting healthy aging by targeting autophagy in ways that account for differences in age, sex, and cell type.
Reference: “Autophagy Flux Is Remodeled Sex- and Cell Type-Specifically During Human Aging, and Is Linked to Reduced Physical Function in Older Adults” by Tatiana M. Moreno, Stephanie R. title: Scientists Discover Chronic Back Pain Can Change How Your Brain Sees You
content:
Scientists have discovered that chronic back pain flares can trigger an unexpected shift in brain activity, engaging regions associated with personal identity and self-reflection. Credit: Shutterstock
A chronic back pain flare may switch on a brain network tied to identity, linking physical pain with how you see yourself.
Researchers at
UC San Diego School of Medicine
found that movement-triggered flares in people with chronic low back pain activated a brain network associated with identity and inward reflection. Painful heat produced the opposite response, suggesting that a familiar back pain flare engages the brain differently from a new external threat.
Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. For people with chronic low back pain (cLBP), which lasts longer than 12 weeks, everyday movements can bring sudden spikes in pain, adding fear and uncertainty to ordinary activities.
The findings, published October 5, 2026, in the
British Journal of Anaesthesia
, offer a possible explanation for why treatments focused on pain symptoms often fall short. They also raise the possibility of treating the relationship between pain and identity.
Two Painful Experiences, Different Brain Responses
The study involved 114 people with cLBP who performed a “leg raise test,” a standard procedure used to provoke back pain. Researchers measured brain blood flow using arterial spin labeling, a specialized functional MRI technique. Participants also received a painful but harmless heat stimulus on the calf, providing a comparison with acute pain from an external source.
Fadel Zeidan, PhD. Credit: Kyle Dykes/ UC San Diego Health Sciences
During movement-triggered flares, the Default Mode Network (DMN) became more active. This collection of connected regions across the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes helps support thoughts about personal identity, memories, and internal feelings. Its involvement in inward reflection has earned it the nickname “self-network.”
Painful heat, by contrast, reduced DMN activity. According to corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, this response allows attention to shift toward an outside threat, such as something hot touching the skin.
“In every pain study, when you’re experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates,” said Zeidan. “What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.”
When Pain Becomes Personal
The brain scans also revealed differences related to pain severity. Participants with worse chronic back pain had stronger connections between the DMN and the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes bodily sensations, including those from the back. More intense pain during the leg raise test corresponded to greater activity in sensory and motor regions, while heart rate increases reliably tracked the intensity of the flare.
Together, these findings suggest that a flare may draw on more than the immediate physical experience. Memories of earlier episodes, expectations about what movement will feel like, and worries about its consequences may all become part of the experience.
“The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It’s contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.”
Why Symptom Relief May Fall Short
The team suspects that these different patterns of brain activity help explain why conventional pain treatments, including opiates, often provide insufficient relief for movement-triggered chronic pain.
“Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that’s not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one’s identity.”
Zeidan’s team has separately investigated
mindfulness meditation
psychedelic compound psilocybin
as approaches that may help people separate pain from their sense of self. Early studies have reported reductions in pain intensity, although larger studies are needed to confirm the benefits and clarify how they occur.
Changing the Relationship with Pain
“These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person,” Zeidan said. “Mindfulness is a meditation technique that’s about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences, and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They’re not a silver bullet—you’re not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you’re changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn’t contaminate your everyday life.”
Zeidan’s laboratory is now conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to examine how mindfulness and psychedelics affect processes involved in thinking about the self. The goal is to understand whether changing those processes can alter how chronic pain is experienced and how much it intrudes on daily life.
Reference: “Brain mechanisms supporting movement-evoked chronic low back pain: an observational brain imaging study” by Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Riegner, Thomas Liu and Fadel Zeidan, 5 October 2026,
British Journal of Anaesthesia
DOI: 10.1016/j.bja.2026.08.010
The study was funded, in part, by the National Institutes of Health’s National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.

title: Cannabis May Be Sabotaging Your Sleep Without You Even Knowing It, Study Finds
content:
Long-term cannabis use may be linked to subtle sleep disturbances that go unnoticed. New research raises questions about its reputation as a sleep aid. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Nearly 35 years of observational data link greater lifetime cannabis use to poorer sleep in middle age, challenging its reputation as a sleep aid.
More than eight hours of sleep might sound like a good night’s rest, but a new Northwestern Medicine study linked recent cannabis use to both a greater likelihood of sleeping that long and more disrupted nights. The fragmented sleep and longer stretches awake recorded by wrist-worn monitors were not reflected in participants’ own sleep ratings, suggesting that people may not notice these disturbances.
The study, published October 9 in
JAMA Network Open
, analyzed data from 1,266 participants in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) Study. This community-based study began in 1985–86 and follows Black and white adults across the U.S.
Researchers repeatedly tracked participants’ cannabis use over nearly 35 years, from young adulthood into middle age. In middle age, participants wore a wrist-based sleep monitor for a week and completed sleep surveys, allowing the team to compare recorded sleep patterns with people’s impressions of their own sleep.
Cannabis users may miss sleep disruptions
Millions of Americans use cannabis as a sleep aid. “This study challenges the common belief that cannabis helps people sleep better,” said corresponding author Dr. Thanh-Huyen T. Vu, research associate professor of preventive medicine (epidemiology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “Our findings suggest cannabis may actually be associated with poorer sleep quality, even if people don’t perceive those changes.”
Greater cumulative cannabis use was associated with lower sleep efficiency, meaning participants spent a smaller percentage of the night asleep. Their sleep was also more fragmented, and they spent more time awake after initially falling asleep. Compared with people who had never used cannabis, recent users showed similar patterns and were significantly more likely to sleep longer than eight hours a night.
“This was one of the most interesting findings,” Vu said of the comparison between the monitor readings and participants’ sleep surveys. “The wearable device detected more nighttime disruption among participants with long-term cannabis exposure, but the participants themselves generally did not report worse sleep.”
Does cannabis cause the sleep disruptions?
The associations with poorer objectively measured sleep remained after researchers accounted for numerous factors known to affect sleep, including age, sex, race, cigarette smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, depression, chronic health conditions, and use of other substances. The study was not designed to determine whether cannabis directly causes sleep problems, so the findings establish an association rather than a causal effect.
“Our data do not support the belief that cannabis is helpful as a sleep aid,” said senior author Mercedes R. Carnethon, chair of the department of preventive medicine at Feinberg. “As cannabis becomes increasingly available and accepted, it’s important to better understand its long-term associations with health behaviors such as sleep.”
The analysis of long-term recreational cannabis use did not distinguish between consumption methods such as smoking and eating edibles. Patterns of cannabis use likely changed over the decades participants were followed, making consumption methods an especially important question for future studies, the authors said.
Regular routines can support better sleep
For people seeking better sleep, well-established strategies can improve sleep quality, said study co-author Kristen L. Knutson, associate professor of neurology (sleep medicine) and preventive medicine (epidemiology) at Feinberg.
“Keep a regular bedtime, make your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and avoid looking at phones and other screens right before bed,” Knutson said. “It can also help to establish a calming routine before sleep, such as reading, meditating or taking a shower. If sleep problems persist, or if you’re a loud snorer, talk with your health care provider to rule out an underlying sleep disorder.”
Reference: “Recent and Cumulative Cannabis Use and Sleep in Middle-Aged Adults” by Thanh-Huyen T. Vu, Kristen L. Knutson, Reto Auer, Julian Jakob, Donald M. Lloyd-Jones and Mercedes R. Carnethon, 9 October 2026,
JAMA Network Open
DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38303
The Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study is conducted and supported by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) in collaboration with the University of Alabama at Birmingham (grants 75N92023D00002 and 75N92023D00005), Northwestern University (grant 75N92023D00004), University of Minnesota (grant 75N92023D00006), and Kaiser Foundation Research Institute (grant 75N92023D00003). The CARDIA Sleep Ancillary Study is funded by grant R01HL152442 from the NHLBI.

title: Inkanva launches a crowdfunding campaign for a perovskite-powered e-paper picture frame
content:
Inkanva launches a crowdfunding campaign for a perovskite-powered e-paper picture frame
Inkanva has launched a Kickstarter campaign for a color e-paper picture frame that it says charges itself from indoor light or sunlight using a flexible perovskite solar panel. At the time of writing, Kickstarter shows it at more than 1,900% of its funding goal, and the company plans to ship in December 2026.
Inkanva is a young company, and this is its first Kickstarter campaign. It describes its product as “color e-paper art for the rooms you live in”: a non-emissive display that reflects ambient light, with interchangeable outer frames. The solar panel is a modular part that attaches to the frame magnetically, which the company says removes the need for a power cable.
Its team page lists a founder, a solar materials scientist formerly at Energy Center Bavaria, and a head of commercialization associated with a flexible perovskite production line. The company says it ran small-batch trial production in July 2026 and expects mass production in October. It has not disclosed its location or funding.
The frame comes in three sizes. The 7.09-inch and 13.3-inch models carry the perovskite panel and have a 1,200 x 1,600 pixel display, according to the campaign. The 28.5-inch model, which has a 2,160 x 3,060 pixel display, is not solar-powered and needs a power outlet. The campaign page lists a Spectra 6 color e-paper display. Inkanva says the frames also have a built-in 5,000 mAh battery, which New Atlas reports lasts up to four months at one image a day when the panel isn’t used.
Images can be loaded through a companion app or a browser on a local network without internet access, with up to 4,000 images in a slideshow. The frames also work with Home Assistant, and the company describes an API that lets AI agents send content to the frame.
Inkanva has not named the supplier of the perovskite panel or disclosed its power output or efficiency, and the products are not yet shipping.

title: Sunic System expects perovskite solar equipment orders for mass production from next year
content:
Sunic System expects perovskite solar equipment orders for mass production from next year
Sunic System
, Korean maker of OLED deposition equipment, says it expects to win orders for mass-production perovskite solar equipment starting next year. CEO Kim Hye-dong said in a recent interview that the first verification results from customers are due at the end of this year, and that he expects perovskite revenue at the end of next year.
The company supplied perovskite solar equipment to overseas customers in July and August. This is said to be dry deposition equipment for the electron transport layer, which supports Gen 8 substrates. Kim said it applies Sunic’s OLED deposition technology to form thin, uniform layers that help move electrons in the cell. He pointed to perovskite’s lower processing temperature than silicon, which can reduce production costs. The company has not named the customers.
Sunic has been building its perovskite business this year. It
partnered with KRICT
on mass-production technology,
set up a U.S. subsidiary
to target perovskite solar commercialization, and
completed the first phase of its Pyeongtaek production hub
. Kim said the company is expanding beyond displays to reduce its dependence on customers’ investment cycles. Sunic’s main business is OLED equipment, including for smart glasses microdisplays.

title: 荒沙地变身光伏绿洲！巴彦淖尔水土保持实现生态产业双赢-索比光伏网
content:
水土保持是生态文明建设的重要基础性工作。近年来，巴彦淖尔市水利局坚守生态保护底线，坚持因地制宜、科学施策，统筹推进水土流失综合治理和生产建设项目水土保持监管工作，持续补齐生态短板、规范项目建设，“十四五”期间累计完成水土流失综合治理面积2200平方公里，水土流失面积由2021年的4.68万平方公里下降至2025年的4.55万平方公里，水土保持率由29.42%提高到31.39%，全市水土流失治理成效持续巩固，生态环境质量稳步提升，实现了生态保护与项目发展双向共赢。
巴彦淖尔市防沙治沙和风电光伏一体化工程临河区20万千瓦光伏项目，正是全市水土保持精细化监管的生动实践。放眼项目现场，光伏板连片排布，沙障规整，林草植被长势良好，一套完备的防风固沙、水土保持防护体系已经成型。据了解，项目建设全过程践行生态优先理念，落实水土保持“三同时”制度，遵循“随坡就势”建设思路，严格管控施工扰动范围，最大限度保护沙地原生植被;裸露开挖土方及时密目网苫盖;光伏板下布设沙障、配套灌溉设施，发挥挡风、固沙、蓄水效能;在沙障区域、升压站周边开展种草、植苗造林，构建综合生态防护体系。在发展清洁能源的同时治理沙地生态，切实实现板上发电、板下固沙、生态增效、产业增收的综合效益。
目前，巴彦淖尔市水土保持工作主要包括水土流失综合治理和生产建设项目水土保持监督管理。坚持两手抓、两促进。一方面积极推进小流域综合治理，以涵养水源，蓄水保土、建立良好的生态环境为目标，切实改善乡村生态与人居环境，惠及广大群众。“十四五”期间共实施28项小流域综合治理项目，总治理面积460公顷，覆盖乌拉特前旗、乌拉特中旗、乌拉特后旗、磴口县、杭锦后旗5个旗县。另一方面不断健全生产建设项目全链条全过程监管体系，严把水土保持方案审批、水土保持补偿费缴纳、“三同时”制度落实、水土保持设施竣工验收等关键关口。要求建设单位依法编制报批水保方案，按标准缴纳水土保持补偿费，严格落实“同时设计、同时施工、同时投产使用”制度，项目投产前完成水土保持设施自主验收、社会公示及报备工作。针对“未批先建”“未批先变”“未批先弃”“未验先投”“治理不达标”等违法行为，依法实施行政处罚，按程序将责任主体纳入水土保持信用“重点关注名单”“黑名单”，以处罚+信用监管联动机制压实企业生态主体责任，从源头遏制人为水土流失。
截至2026年9月底，市级审批生产建设项目水土保持方案60项，受理水土保持设施自主验收报备24项。
水土保持相关规定的落实不是“卡项目”，而是为发展“保长远”。水土保持功在当代，利在千秋，巴彦淖尔市水利局将持续做好水土保持各项工作，统筹生态保护与产业发展，守护好河套大地的沃土清流。

title: 天津：“十五五”时期新增用电需求全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决-索比光伏网
content:
10月22日上午，天津市政府新闻办举行“开局起步‘十五五’”系列主题新闻发布会，介绍“十五五”时期我市能源发展有关情况。市发展改革委主任梁军、市发展改革委副主任刘涛、市工业和信息化局副局长蔡讴、国网天津市电力公司副总经理庄剑、中国海油天津公司副总经理谢日彬出席，介绍有关情况并回答媒体关心的问题。
梁军介绍，能源保障和安全事关国计民生。“十四五”以来，天津深入践行“四个革命、一个合作”能源安全新战略，着力强基础、调结构、优布局、育动能，能源高质量发展迈出坚实步伐。“十四五”期间，能源发展成效主要体现在四个方面。一是保障能力更强，渤海油田稳居全国第一大原油生产基地，原油增量占全国总增量的约40%。电力供应水平稳步提高，电力装机较2020年增长73.7%。二是能源结构更绿，新能源超过煤电成为第一大电源，煤炭消费比重由34.6%下降至24.6%，非化石能源消费比重由7.1%提高至17%，绿电交易连续三年倍速增长。三是设施布局更优，天然气主干架构持续巩固，三座LNG接收站投产运行，接收能力领跑全国。特高压输电网络加速构建，500千伏电网建成双环网结构。四是发展动能更新，获批京津冀燃料电池汽车示范城市群，打造天津港保税区氢能示范产业园，依托荣程集团等企业加快交通领域氢能应用场景建设，燃料电池实证试验平台纳入国家首批能源领域氢能试点，“制储运加用”氢能全产业链发展格局加快形成。
“十五五”时期是我国加快构建新型能源体系、建设能源强国的重要时期。我们将认真落实党中央决策部署和国家发展改革委、国家能源局工作要求，以保安全、优结构、强产业、降成本为主线，着力打造区域能源保障枢纽和能源领域新质生产力发展引领区，到2030年，初步建成以非化石能源为增量供应主体、化石能源为兜底保障、新型电力系统为关键支撑、绿色智慧节约为用能导向的清洁低碳安全高效的新型能源体系，更好支撑经济社会高质量发展。为了实现以上目标，我们在任务安排方面突出“四个着力”。
一是着力筑牢能源安全根基，全面提升综合保障能力。加强与煤炭主产区合作，扎实做好煤炭稳供保运。大力推动渤海油田、大港油田稳产增储，打造全国油气资源保障供给中心和重要LNG接收区;建成天津LNG外输管道复线等项目，持续巩固国产气、进口气相结合，陆上气、LNG相补充的多源多向供气保障格局。健全多层次能源储备体系，强化天然气、成品油、煤炭等能源储备，扎实推进大港油田储气库群项目建设，力争储气库工作气量达到50亿立方米。增强供热、燃气综合保障能力，改造供热管网3000公里以上、燃气管网2000公里以上。
二是着力推进绿色低碳发展，强化生产消费协同转型。统筹推进风电、光伏等非化石能源开发，实施蓟州“风光火热储”多能互补一体化等试点，非化石能源发电装机超过2000万千瓦，装机比重超过50%;持续扩大省间绿电交易，谋划新增绿电入津通道，“十五五”时期新增用电需求全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决。全面落实大气污染治理攻坚行动部署，加快化石能源消费绿色转型，高水平高质量做好节能降碳，煤炭消费总量较2025年下降10%、比重降至21%左右，非化石能源消费比重增至22.2%。
三是着力构建新型电力系统，推进供给水平质效双升。发挥好传统火电兜底保障作用，进一步提高外受电规模，有序实施杨柳青电厂、大唐盘山电厂容量替代，电力装机超过4000万千瓦。抢抓“六张网”建设机遇，打造新型电网平台，建成大同—天津南特高压交流输电工程，推进黑龙江—天津特高压直流输电工程实施，构建“三交一直”特高压输电网络;建设500千伏加强型双环网，推进电网数字化智能化转型。加快蓟州龙潭沟、西大峪抽水蓄能电站开工建设，统筹布局200万千瓦新型储能电站，推进长时储能与快速响应协同联动。提升需求侧协同能力，创新发展虚拟电厂、算电协同、车网互动等新业态。
四是着力推进科技产业创新，前瞻布局发展未来能源。发展壮大新一代风电光伏，打造风电高端装备制造产业集群、全国领先的硅片—光伏组件一体化制造业集群。积极提升新型储能产业能级，前瞻布局固态电池、钠离子电池等新型储能产业。加快构建氢能全链条产业生态，抢抓京津冀城市群氢能综合应用试点机遇，加快输氢、加氢基础设施建设，有序拓展交通、石化、建筑、钢铁等领域用氢场景，高标准建设天津港保税区氢能产业园，壮大氢能装备产业集群。培育发展绿氨、绿色甲醇、可持续航空燃料产业，打造北方国际航运绿色液体燃料加注贸易物流中心。
下一步，我们将锚定发展目标，聚焦能源强国战略导向和“双碳”要求，全力加快全市新型能源体系建设，推动区域能源保障枢纽能级持续提升、能源领域新质生产力发展聚势增效，为全面建设社会主义现代化大都市、奋力谱写中国式现代化天津篇章提供坚实能源支撑，为能源强国建设贡献天津力量。

title: 青海落地绿电溯源地方标准-索比光伏网
content:
据新华社报道，记者从国网青海省电力公司获悉，经过为期三个月的验证，10月22日青海省正式落地《用电企业绿电溯源方法》专项地方标准，标志着青海在绿色电力消费量化管控、全流程溯源体系建设方面实现新突破。
作为全国重要的清洁能源产业基地，青海清洁能源装机占比、绿电发电量占比均居全国前列。随着绿色算力、绿色制造产业快速崛起，用电企业对绿电消费核算与溯源认证的需求日益增加。为破解绿电溯源难题、提升绿电消费可信度，国网青海省电力公司自2024年启动标准前期研究，联合青海大学等科研单位，组建标准编制组，推进标准研究制定。
编制组立足青海省清洁能源产业实际，开展典型区域电网运行数据采集与用电负荷特性调研，收集整理光伏、风电等绿电项目出力曲线、上网电量及输配电路径等关键参数，梳理青海省绿电交易、溯源平台运行及绿色算力评价的实践经验与数据基础，建立绿电流数据模型，逐步构建全链条、全覆盖的绿电溯源技术体系。
截至目前，依托绿电溯源成果，青海已建成全省992家企业的“碳账户”，有效支撑“碳账户”贷款发放，推动绿色金融精准服务低碳企业。

title: US Wind Maryland project faces new federal offshore wind review
content:
US Wind Maryland project faces new federal offshore wind review TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
US Wind Maryland project faces new federal offshore wind review
The US government has filed a motion seeking re-evaluation of the Bureau
of Ocean Energy Management's (BOEM) approval of US Wind's Maryland Offshore
Wind Project, while also requesting summary judgment on the remaining claims
against federal agencies.
In court filings, the US Department of the Interior said the project's
Construction and Operations Plan (COP) approval should be returned to the
agency for further review under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA).
According to the filing, the Department of the Interior said the original
analysis did not properly explain how the project's impacts on other users
of the Outer Continental Shelf complied with statutory requirements.
BOEM's review identified potential impacts on the North Atlantic right
whale, scenic and visual resources, commercial fisheries, and scientific
research activities. Despite those findings, the agency approved the project
and concluded that it balanced offshore wind development objectives with
other ocean uses.
The filing follows a series of legal challenges involving the US offshore
wind sector, most recently the US government's cross-motion for summary
judgment in litigation concerning Ørsted's Revolution
Wind project,
reported earlier this month.

title: National Grid awards Birkhill Wood Substation contract to Balfour Beatty
content:
International infrastructure group Balfour Beatty has been selected by
National Grid to deliver the first phase of the Birkhill Wood 400 kV substation
project.
The contract includes the development of the detailed design and site preparation
works ahead of construction, which is scheduled to begin next year.
The award has been made under National Grid’s £8 billion Electricity Transmission
Partnership. Balfour Beatty was appointed to the framework in 2025 as the
delivery partner for projects in the North East of England.
Tony Wilson, managing director of Balfour Beatty’s Power Transmission
& Distribution business, said: “Upgrading the UK's electricity network
is essential to connecting more renewable energy and meeting future demand
for secure, low-carbon power.
“We are pleased to continue our partnership with National Grid, drawing
on our extensive experience and expertise to deliver the Early Contractor
Involvement.”
Once completed, the Birkhill Wood 400 kV substation is expected to play
a key role in supporting the UK’s renewable energy transition by strengthening
the electricity network and connecting three North Sea wind farms.
Construction is currently expected to begin in 2027, with commissioning
scheduled for 2030. Third party connections to the substation are planned
for the fourth quarter of that year.

title: Petrovietnam strengthens offshore wind partnerships during Denmark visit
content:
Within the context of a state visit to Denmark by Vietnam’s General Secretary
and President To Lam, Petrovietnam advanced agreements with Danish partners,
including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP).
The agreement relates to the Nam Trung Bo 1 offshore wind project and follows
a joint development agreement signed by the companies in August 2025.
The project remains in the early stages of development. However, according
to a previous announcement from CIP, the offshore wind farm is expected
to support Vietnam’s green energy transition while creating long-term
economic value.
In addition, PTSC Marine Mechanical Services Co., Ltd. (PTSC M&C) and
Semco Maritime A/S have agreed to strengthen their strategic cooperation
between 2026 and 2030 in the offshore wind substation sector.
The partnership aims to support the development of offshore wind infrastructure
and expand international supply chain opportunities.

title: Archer pauses shareholder distributions amid wind project disputes
content:
Archer has reported third quarter EBITDA of $44.2 million, despite ongoing
commercial disputes related to the Culzean
EPC wind project.
According to the announcement the disputes remain unresolved even though
the project's main deliveries have been completed.
The company said negotiations with the client over material variation orders,
as well as a claim against a subcontractor, have taken longer than anticipated.
Archer added that the timing and value of any potential recoveries remain
uncertain.
As a result, Archer has temporarily paused shareholder distributions and
said it expects to revisit the programme in early 2027 as leverage levels
decline and visibility around the outstanding matters improves.
Archer also said it will not pursue further offshore wind EPC projects
and will instead evaluate strategic options for Archer Wind, including
a partial or full divestment.
The TotalEnergies Culzean project is located in the UK, with 3 MW expected
capacity.

title: Nexans wins key role in Mallorca-Menorca interconnection project
content:
Red Eléctrica has selected Nexans as the preferred supplier for the strategic
Mallorca-Menorca 3 interconnection project.
Under the agreement, Nexans will support Red Eléctrica, Spain’s electricity
transmission system operator, with the development of the project. The
company will also provide engineering services for a comprehensive cable
system incorporating both subsea and onshore infrastructure.
“The Mallorca-Menorca interconnection is an important infrastructure investment
that will help reinforce network resilience and support the energy transition
in the Balearic Islands,” said Pascal Radue, executive vice president
of PWR-Transmission at Nexans.
According to the company, the agreement marks the start of the engineering
phase for a new 132 kV HVAC cable link between Mallorca and Menorca. The
project is expected to strengthen the connection between the two islands
and enhance the long-term reliability of the regional power system.
Nexans said environmental stewardship will remain a key focus throughout
both the planning and execution phases of the project, reflecting the ecological
sensitivity of the area.

title: VC Firms Tap LP Pools, Warehouse Loans for Speedy AI Cash
content: When Reflection AI set out to raise $2.5 billion early this year, one of its existing venture backers, B Capital, was eager to invest again in the startup, which has emerged as the most high-profile U.S. maker of open-source AI models. But Reflection’s valuation had more than tripled in just six months, forcing investors to write big checks for a sizable stake. Such a check would have been too big for B Capital’s main venture fund, a $500 million vehicle raised in July. To come up with the cash, the company turned to a different source of capital: a pool of money apart from its regular fund, designed to give limited partners — the pension funds, endowments and wealthy individuals that back VC firms—more direct access to hot startups like Reflection at reduced fees. This strategy, known as limited partner co-investing, has become increasingly popular during the last few years as funding rounds in startups have jumped in both size and frequency. It’s just one of the ways VC firms are adapting to the immense cash demands of the AI boom. Those changes also include VC firms raising funds more frequently. They’re also taking out warehouse loans, lines of credit typically used by private equity firms. Venture capitalists are starting to tap these to come up with cash to invest in startups before the VC firms have raised money from their limited partners. For B Capital, a VC firm led by Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin and two other tech investors, the limited partner co-investment pool meant the VC firm could invest $100 million in Reflection AI—double the size of what it had previously invested in the company, according to a person with direct knowledge of the investment. VC firms have increasingly turned to such pools as startup fundraising rounds have swelled to billions of dollars at a time. The pooled limited partner funds differ from general VC funds because they tend to back just a few startups rather than the dozen-plus a more traditional fund might invest in. Limited partners have sought out these investments to get more exposure to breakout stars in venture firms’ portfolios, such as Anthropic and OpenAI. An added plus for limited partners: VC funds typically waive or reduce their fees on money raised from limited partners for these direct or co-investments. B Capital, for instance, sometimes offers co-investment opportunities with no management fee and a 10% performance fee, often known as carried interest, as opposed to the 2% management fee and 20% performance fee traditional for most VC funds, according to the person. The co-investment pools also mean there’s money ready when the startup signals it’s raising again. In the past, a VC firm could spend a few weeks negotiating one-off agreements with individual limited partners to come up with enough cash to invest in a hot startup. These days, such lengthy negotiations could cause an investment firm to lose its allocation—the right to invest in a company—say venture capitalists and limited partners. B Capital is far from the only VC firm to have pursued this strategy. Lightspeed Venture Partners brought limited partners into over $5 billion worth of co-investments over the last five years, according to a person with knowledge of its investments. Lightspeed used that money to invest in Anthropic and other startups alongside investments from its general funds. The firm typically waived management fees and reduced carried interest fees for the limited partner co-investments. Thrive Capital has invited limited partners to co-invest while it has led huge funding rounds into companies including OpenAI . For instance, CalPERS—the California pension fund giant—invested in a Thrive special purpose vehicle that raised over $744 million to invest in Stripe in 2023. VC firms are coming up with creative solutions to keep up with the steep cash needs of AI startups. Startup fundraises of over $100 million made up over 87% of all the money invested by VC firms in the first half of the year, according to data firm PitchBook. To meet their needs, some of the largest VC firms, including Thrive Capital, General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz , have in the past year raised new funds less than two years after their last fundraising, bucking the typical two- to three-year cadence typical of most VC funds. Megafunds are “constantly out there keeping checkwriters warm in advance of quickly raising a new fund,” said Peter Werner, chair of law firm Cooley’s global business department. Warehouse Loans VC firms are also beginning to explore other tactics that have been more popular with other types of investment firms, such as PE and real estate managers. JP Morgan Chase is among the banks working with VC firms to make warehouse loans, a short- to medium-term revolving line of credit that can help the firms invest before they’ve secured the capital to do so, according to someone familiar with the bank’s thinking. Warehouse loans also let the borrower take on some leverage, which can boost investment returns by minimizing the initial cash the firms must put forward to close investments. A handful of VC funds are also classified as registered investment advisers, a designation that makes it easier to use short-term debt because it removes restrictions on how much debt a given firm can hold. Warehouse loans are different from capital call credit lines , a type of loan VC firms have used for years. The firms draw on such credit lines after they’ve received commitments from limited partners for money but before the money has hit their account. “The need to move at lightning speed to capitalize on some of these opportunities” is driving demand for loans, said Cooley’s Werner.

title: Ramp Investors Went Nuclear Against Airwallex After Doomed Deal
content: In April 2025, Eric Glyman, co-founder and co-CEO of Ramp, received some bad news: A deal was falling apart. Glyman had been hoping Ramp, a highly valued startup that sells corporate credit cards and expense management software, could strike a partnership with Airwallex—a fast-growing fintech founded in Melbourne, Australia—that would improve Ramp’s ability to handle international payments. But now Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang was pulling the plug on the proposed deal—partly because of pressure from investors who wanted his company to compete with Ramp, according to employees of both companies. Glyman made an attempt to salvage the partnership, according to people familiar with discussions between the two companies. Zhang demurred. Soon after, Glyman warned Zhang that the relationship between their companies might not be so friendly in the future, according to people familiar with the situation. In the wake of the canceled deal, some of Ramp’s high-profile, politically connected investors have launched a public and private campaign to urge the U.S. government to saddle Airwallex with a government investigation that probes any links the company may have with the Chinese government. Those investors have alleged that the Chinese government could access customer data passing through Airwallex subsidiaries in China. The campaign against Airwallex brings into stark relief how the current geopolitical climate makes it possible for a company’s adversaries to weaponize perceived ties to China against it. The fact that the fight is happening between two startups in the unglamorous expense and money-processing businesses underscores how fierce the competition can get in what might otherwise appear to be a sleepy corner of tech. Airwallex sells a web-based platform to businesses for sending and receiving international payments. Many of the 11-year-old company’s earliest investors were Chinese firms, and during its early years, a large chunk of its staff—including many of its senior leaders—and the majority of its customers were based in China. It continues to maintain a sizable operation in mainland China, though it has never been headquartered there. One of the Ramp investors who has been working on the campaign against Airwallex is venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale, co-founder of Palantir. Lonsdale has coordinated with a political operative network partially funded by conservative activist Leonard Leo to lobby state and federal lawmakers to investigate Airwallex, according to people briefed on Lonsdale’s private remarks. Airwallex CEO and co-founder Jack Zhang. (Getty Images) That network includes State Armor Action, a think tank launched in 2024 and funded by an entity associated with Leo, according to public donor filings. State Armor, which is based in Austin, Texas, is led by Michael Lucci. Over the last year, Lucci has urged Texas lawmakers and a House of Representatives committee devoted to China to probe Airwallex in legislative hearings and through publicly released letters. Lucci was previously a senior fellow at the Cicero Institute, a think tank founded by Lonsdale. Lonsdale, Lucci and Leo did not respond to requests for comment. In addition to Lonsdale, Ramp has other high-profile investors like Founders Fund and Thrive Capital, who’ve excitedly watched the startup’s valuation soar—from $13 billion in March 2025 to $60 billion in fundraising announced this month. Its sharp-elbowed feud with Airwallex presents a real contrast to the public perception Ramp enjoys as a happy-go-lucky disruptor of a staid industry. It has reinforced that image with cutesy marketing stunts, such as its hiring of skateboarder Tony Hawk to ride a Ramp-branded half-pipe outside the New York Stock Exchange. (Glyman would not comment for this story.) Ramp co-CEO and co-founder Eric Glyman. (Getty Images) The battle comes at a key moment for Airwallex. Its valuation has risen quickly, too—from $8 billion in December 2025 to $11 billion in June this year—and it has its own collection of prominent investors, like T. Rowe Price and Baillie Gifford, a large European money management firm. To keep growing, the startup has been hoping to seize more business for itself in America, eyeing a potential IPO. In December 2025, it said it would crown another headquarters beyond its existing one in Singapore—on Spear Street in San Francisco’s Financial District. To mount a defense against the attacks, Airwallex has brought on former U.S. Attorney General Bill Barr as an adviser and lobbyist. “Global banking and payments companies operate internationally as a matter of course, with teams and operations across multiple markets. That is not in itself a basis for suspicion,” said Barr. He criticized the efforts to spark U.S. government investigations into Airwallex as “deeply inappropriate.…Our national security professionals have serious threats to contend with, and their time and resources should not be diverted by Silicon Valley rivalries.” A Deal Gone Bad Partnership discussions between Ramp and Airwallex began around 2023 when Airwallex approached Ramp for help solving a problem. Ramp’s focus on the U.S. market had left it vulnerable to competitors that have global payments licenses and other capabilities for moving money around the world. Its operation wasn’t as far-reaching, and it hoped a partnership with Airwallex would enable it to add more international customers. Ramp wanted to structure the deal so it could promise customers that none of their data would be stored in China or handled by Chinese staff. The talks fell apart when Airwallex told Ramp it wasn’t possible for international payments to be handled strictly by its U.S. operations if those customers were in China or Hong Kong—payments sent overseas would have to involve Airwallex’s subsidiaries around the world. (An Airwallex spokesperson said that staff based in China and Hong Kong can’t access U.S. customer data and such an arrangement goes beyond U.S. government requirements.) No deal was signed, and discussions between Ramp and Airwallex fell away until they resumed in 2025. As Ramp and Airwallex began talking again, some of Airwallex’s investors grew unhappy about the brewing partnership. They were eager for Airwallex to compete directly with Ramp, wary of how Ramp handled cross-border transactions and aspects of its offshore corporate credit card business, people familiar with the situation said. After Zhang pulled the plug on the partnership in April 2025, Airwallex launched an expense management and corporate card product the following month that seeks to rival Ramp’s own flagship product in the U.S. A Ramp spokesperson said that the companies were unable to agree on legal terms. Keith Rabois, a Ramp board director and investor, said he thinks Airwallex withdrew because it feared a Ramp deal would expose Airwallex’s inability to shield data from the Chinese government. “It’s unprecedented for a company to walk away from a negotiation at the last minute based upon a request for data protection assurances without proposing an alternative,” Rabois said. An Airwallex spokesperson disputed Rabois’ analysis of the events. “We walked away from a commercial relationship with Ramp in 2025 because we knew our competing products would complicate our relationship…during contract discussions, Ramp asked questions about data access and storage. We answered those questions, and Ramp was fully prepared to move forward,” said the spokesperson. “We understand this was not the outcome the Ramp team wanted, but it was the right strategic decision for Airwallex.” The ‘Oppo Smear’ The first sign of political trouble for Airwallex came in December 2025 when Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, a vocal critic of China, issued a public letter urging then–Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate whether the Chinese Communist Party could access Airwallex data. According to a person close to the company, Zhang was caught off guard when he learned of Cotton’s efforts shortly after leaving lunch with an investor in London. Around the same time, Rabois wrote a post on X that criticized Airwallex as “a Chinese backdoor into sensitive American data.” (Rabois’ husband is U.S. Under Secretary of State Jacob Helberg, who previously campaigned to ban TikTok over its Chinese ties.) Then, a month ago, Rep. John Moolenaar, chair of the House committee on China, sent a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging an investigation into Airwallex and published the letter publicly. Rabois and Lonsdale, a prominent Republican donor, amplified the letter online through posts on X, while another Ramp adviser and shareholder—Lulu Cheng Meservey, a widely followed public relations operative—alleged in a post on X that Airwallex was “under investigation for enabling ccp access to financial data.” (Meservey declined to elaborate on any knowledge she had of an investigation, saying in an email that she hasn’t “followed Senator Cotton’s concerns closely.”) Venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale, an investor in Ramp, has been an active force in the efforts to spark investigations into Airwallex, a Ramp rival. (Getty Images) The Treasury Department has not said whether it is investigating Airwallex. According to an Airwallex spokesperson, a recent assessment of its data handling by Coalfire, a Chicago-based cybersecurity firm, concluded that Airwallex has “robust” controls to prevent unauthorized access of customer data by employees or vendors in China and Hong Kong. One Lonsdale X post also mentioned Rippling, another valuable U.S.-based fintech that competes with Ramp. In the post , Lonsdale insinuated that Rippling might have a partnership with Airwallex—and that Rippling customers should be concerned about the Chinese government getting access to some data. In a reply to Lonsdale’s post, Rippling CEO and co-founder Parker Conrad said his company doesn’t have a relationship with Airwallex and labeled Lonsdale’s remarks against Airwallex as “an oppo smear by Ramp.” He was referring to opposition research, a tactic used in both politics and the corporate world to dig up information on a company that would present it in a bad light. Often such campaigns are rooted in a few facts and a good amount of media spin. A Rise in China Zhang’s investors and supporters see him as a rags-to-riches entrepreneur whose unrelenting work ethic has turned Airwallex into a fast-growing startup with an enviable reach through the global financial system. In the third quarter of this year, Airwallex hit $1.5 billion in annualized revenue by facilitating payments for China-based e-commerce companies and becoming an international payments platform for fast-growing startups such as Brex and Deel. Along with major U.S. and European investors, Airwallex has attracted some of the largest venture capitalists in Australia, where producing a unicorn startup has been a rarity. Several years ago, Stripe offered $1.2 billion for the company. Zhang turned down the offer. Zhang moved from Qingdao, China, to Australia in 2000 at age 15 to attend high school, living with a host family. Shortly after, his banker father, who remained in China with the rest of Zhang’s family, lost his job and couldn’t financially support Zhang anymore. When Zhang got to college, he earned money with a series of odd jobs—washing dishes, bartending and clerking at a gas station. After graduating, Zhang developed trading systems for National Australia Bank, a major financial institution in the country. He kept up side hustles exporting olive oil and wine and developing real estate that delivered him a nest egg worth about $10 million, he said in a 2025 podcast interview . In 2015, he decided to launch Airwallex while running a coffee shop in Melbourne: He’d gotten the idea for a startup that could simplify sending money across borders after he ran into difficulties buying cups and coffee beans overseas using traditional banks and payment methods. Zhang assembled a plan for Airwallex with the help of three friends he’d met at the University of Melbourne: Max Li, Ki-lok Wong and Jacob Dai, all of whom became co-founders. Li discussed the concept for Airwallex with Lucy Yueting Liu, a young former investment consultant for China International Capital Corp., a large Chinese investment bank, who invested $1 million. She became a co-founder as well and served as the company’s first chief operating officer. (Airwallex’s founders hold Australian citizenship, and Liu holds a New Zealand passport). Airwallex early backers included Chinese groups such as Hong Kong–based Gobi Zhiying and Tencent. (In 2025, the U.S. government designated Tencent a Chinese military company.) Sequoia’s former Chinese venture arm also invested. GOP Rep. John Moolenaar has urged the Treasury Department to investigate Airwallex. (Getty Images) In 2018, Shanghai-based Huashan Capital sued Airwallex, alleging that Zhang had failed to pay for shares he had bought back from the investor. The case was settled, and Huashan is no longer an investor. That same year, Airwallex, which Zhang incorporated in the Cayman Islands, moved its headquarters from Melbourne to Hong Kong, in part to apply for a banking license. Its main customers at the time were in China and Southeast Asia, and they included JD.com , the Chinese e-commerce giant. Often Airwallex would fly new employees hired in the U.S. to its offices in China to meet senior executives. As the company grew, workers based in China sometimes clashed with the Western employees, who had a more laid-back approach, said several former employees. Staff dedicated to financial crimes compliance who were based outside China sometimes argued with Airwallex’s China-based sales employees about how to handle financial and legal risks, those former employees said. Soon, Airwallex focused on expanding outside of China. In 2023, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore. Its series of recent fundraisings has shifted the makeup of its cap table and diminished the prominence of its early Chinese investors. Tencent now holds less than 10% of the company and has no access to information beyond those of any other minority shareholder, according to Airwallex. About a quarter of the company’s staff is now based in China, and a third of the company’s revenue now comes from Europe and the U.S. Last January, the company faced a round of negative press in Australia after the country’s anti–money-laundering regulator ordered an audit of Airwallex’s financial crime controls. That bad press came just after Airwallex had sent legal letters to several Australia publications, hoping to get those outlets to remove stories they had published about its workplace and its handling of financial crime controls, including some stories from years earlier, according to people familiar with the matter. Allies in America To respond to the assault in the U.S. by Ramp’s investors, Airwallex has called in the cavalry. Barr, the former U.S. attorney general for Presidents George H.W. Bush and Donald Trump, recently lobbied the Department of Justice on behalf of Airwallex, according to lobbying disclosures. The company’s representatives met with Senator Cotton’s staff in July to assuage his concerns and met with other members of the executive branch and in Congress, according to people briefed on the meetings. And to combat what it sees as unfair media coverage, the company has enlisted law firm Clare Locke, now known for handling legal matters for prominent people and companies in the Trump orbit, according to people familiar with the matter. To further build a presence in America, Airwallex is now an advertising sponsor of “All-In,” the podcast hosted by venture capitalists Chamath Palihapitiya, David Sacks, David Friedberg and Jason Calacanis. And during the latest season of Major League Baseball, Airwallex became the official jersey patch sponsor for the San Francisco Giants baseball team, replacing the logo of a venerable American icon: Chevrolet.

title: Anthropic’s Elevator Problem: Persuading Investors to Share Its AI Dream
content: One quotation has rattled around in my head for a while, which I first heard from early Anthropic investor Jaan Tallinn: “The future of the world will be decided by a group of people who fit in an elevator.” The enigmatic billionaire said on a podcast earlier this year that a friend had used the illustration to describe the concentration of power at the leading AI companies. I’ve been reflecting on it as Anthropic prepares for its Wall Street debut because the company’s small group of powerful insiders, who are set to realize incredible wealth at unprecedented speed, face their biggest test in explaining themselves to the world outside their elevator. To raise the money Anthropic leaders need, and to keep raising it again and again, big fund managers need to fully buy in. This is the stark divide worth watching as Anthropic’s IPO gets closer, with a prospectus likely to drop in the coming days en route to a listing expected next month. Anthropic employees and executives, closest to the action and with the most to gain, have deep faith about the power of AI and its ability to take over all kinds of work and make scientific breakthroughs that will power the company’s success for years to come. For instance, the company published in a little-noticed report last week, titled “ AI Expectations Gap ,” that 91% of the 1,300 Anthropic employees surveyed believed AI would be able to make a Nobel Prize-level breakthrough by 2030, compared to 39% of Americans surveyed. Another report released the same day about how Anthropic’s own jobs are changing said hours worked by AI agents inside the company outnumbered human employees six to one. Wall Street, meanwhile, doesn’t have the same conviction about the future of the AI industry that it will need to keep funding. You see the anxiety and gyrations around AI cloud companies, semiconductor firms and cybersecurity stocks. You also see it in the reaction to Anthropic's meeting last week with potential investors , some of whom came away thinking that its rapid growth isn't enough to justify the IPO valuation of nearly $2 trillion that some bankers have floated privately. As things stand, Anthropic would be going public as Wall Street confidence on AI is the lowest it has been all year. Even numbers-oriented corporate finance executives at the big companies most likely to tout the benefits of AI—the big banks getting paid big fees to take Anthropic and other AI giants public—still stop short of laying out the hard-and-fast financial upside of the technology. “The benefits aren't observable in our current quarterly earnings,” JPMorgan finance chief Jeremy Barnum said on an analyst call last week, before clarifying his personal excitement about the technology’s potential. “So how long is it going to take for that to show up? We'll see. And obviously, some of those benefits are going to be offset by token costs, which is a whole other conversation,” Barnum added. These are the conversations Amodei and other Anthropic executives will need to have in the coming weeks, as they have to convince investors they have can tackle their most obvious challenge: increasing competition from open-source AI models that do a lot of white-collar work well enough for a fraction of the price Anthropic charges. The company, despite its jaw-dropping growth, still faces doubts that it will ever achieve the kind of business dominance that investors truly salivate over. Peter Thiel, the tech investor who once wrote that “competition is for losers,” said on Walter Isaacson’s podcast this week that the AI business remains a heated race. “It’s the furthest thing from a monopoly imaginable,” he said. He added that while Anthropic had grabbed the lead from OpenAI, “it also still feels that Google and Meta and Grok are not that far behind. I'm not sure China is that far behind.” That leaves some big future questions hanging over this IPO: Will Anthropic lose its lead? And if it does, how will the company respond? How will Wall Street? I spoke to several current and former employees, as well as Anthropic executives, while profiling Amodei over the summer . The company’s most unusual trait—and potential blind spot—is its quasi-religious faith in Amodei to guide all of them into the singularity, or the time when AI exceeds human capabilities. His power appears to come from not only creating a culture of free-flowing candor, but also a track record of accurate predictions. Right now, Anthropic, and Amodei himself, seem to vibrate with confidence. Big money managers who attended the investor day in San Francisco last week called his presentation “uplifting.” In the coming weeks, that confident performance could very well help assuage a wary Wall Street. Or Amodei could take for granted that investors aren’t nearly as certain about the near-term economic power of AI as he is—or as anyone who fits inside Anthropic’s elevator every day. title: Why Blackstone Thinks AI Bottlenecks Could Work in its Favor
content: Greetings! On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem—Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant—repeated a version of that refrain. On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry’s expansion could actually work in Blackstone’s favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn’t signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. Blackstone’s third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called “extraordinary” data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. “Despite all the negative things you’re reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we’re driving the highest returns,” Gray said during the call. But it’s hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave’s stock and bond prices plunging—the neocloud’s shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week—while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google’s TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn’t undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. “We’re continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute,” Gray said. While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry’s broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it’s not clear where all the money will come from. Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone’s push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. “We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from,” he said at The Information’s AI Agenda event in San Francisco. Data Center Headwinds Despite Blackstone’s overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Meta Platforms’ stock fell 7% as investor enthusiasm over its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday gave way to concerns about the probability that it will need to issue new equity to pay for its AI spending. Andreessen Horowitz renamed its flagship blockchain fund a16z Frontier, dropping “crypto” from its name (The Information’s earlier scoop on the change is here ). Google partnered with energy company Voltus to pay homes and businesses to use less electricity during periods of peak demand. title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps
content: Salesforce is leading the software industry’s attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce’s built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms’ apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates—which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents—and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven’t yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps’ built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers’ AI agents haven’t started charging the tolls. They’re letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company’s website , Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable “interaction,” according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn’t clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person’s computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn’t announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce’s own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they’re reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce’s apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won’t affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable “interactions,” customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a “headless license,” a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce’s new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce’s built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, Lumen made a “major” investment in using Salesforce’s AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen’s human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been “super flexible” about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives.
